posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Scale Up Without Slowing Down
posts.subtitle: Give each token only a few experts to think with, not the whole model.
posts.summary: Mixture of Experts replaces a dense feed-forward block with many smaller expert blocks plus a learned router that activates only a handful per token. This decouples total model capacity from per-token compute cost, letting models scale to huge parameter counts cheaply — at the price of harder training and heavier memory/communication demands at serving time.

slides.title: The Trick Behind Trillion-Parameter Models
slides.body: Mixture of Experts (MoE) lets a model have enormous total capacity while only 'thinking' with a small slice of it on any given token.

slides.title: Dense Models Pay for Every Parameter, Every Token
slides.body: A dense transformer's feed-forward layers activate 100% of their weights for every single token, no matter how simple that token is.
bullets: Dense feed-forward blocks run the full matrix multiply for every token — there's no 'this token doesn't need all this math' shortcut.
Compute per token scales directly with total parameters: roughly double the params, roughly double the FLOPs per token.
Labs wanted trillion-parameter capacity without a trillion-parameter inference bill.

slides.title: Route Each Token to a Few Specialist Experts
slides.body: MoE swaps the single dense FFN for many smaller 'expert' FFNs plus a tiny gating network that picks which experts handle each token.
bullets: A router — a small learned layer — scores every expert for a token and selects only the top-k highest scoring ones (commonly k=1 or k=2).
Only the selected experts run their FFN on that token; every unselected expert contributes zero compute for it.
Total parameters across all experts can be huge, while the active compute per token stays small.

slides.title: The Hard Part Is Keeping Experts Balanced
slides.body: The routing math is simple; the engineering problem is making sure every expert actually gets trained and used.
bullets: Switch Transformer (Google, 2021) used top-1 routing — just 1 of N experts per token — to scale past a trillion parameters while keeping per-token compute comparable to a far smaller dense model.
Each expert has a capacity (max tokens it can accept per batch); tokens that overflow get dropped or sent to a fallback — a real quality tradeoff, not a free lunch.
An auxiliary load-balancing loss penalizes the router whenever it funnels too many tokens to the same few experts, preventing 'expert collapse.'

slides.title: Same Compute, Very Different Capacity
slides.body: Mixtral 8x7B makes the tradeoff concrete: most of its parameters sit idle on any given token.

slides.title: Watch a Router Specialize — Without Being Told To
slides.body: Picture an MoE model processing: "The patient's white blood cell count was elevated."
bullets: The router may learn to send tokens like 'patient' and 'blood' toward experts that, through gradient descent alone, drifted toward medical vocabulary.
Feed the same model "The hedge fund's short position was elevated" and 'hedge' and 'position' can land on entirely different experts — no human labeled any of this.
Caveat: real routing is usually messier than clean topic specialization — it often splits more by syntax or token frequency — but the mechanism is identical either way.

slides.title: The Bill Comes Due in Memory and Infrastructure
slides.body: MoE trades compute for complexity — and that complexity shows up in serving memory and training infrastructure, not model quality.
bullets: Memory doesn't shrink: every expert must stay resident across your GPUs even though a token only touches a couple — Mixtral still has to hold all 8 experts, not just the 2 it uses.
Distributed training needs all-to-all GPU communication to ship each token to the right expert's device — a genuine network bottleneck at scale (expert parallelism).
Fine-tuning is twitchy: a learning-rate or data shift can trigger router collapse, where most tokens pile onto 1-2 experts and the rest go stale.
Skip MoE for small models or single-GPU serving — there's no spare memory budget or distributed infrastructure to amortize the routing overhead against.

slides.title: Capacity and Compute, Decoupled
bullets: MoE decouples total parameters from per-token compute: huge capacity, small active compute per token.
A router picks the top-k experts per token; everything hinges on an auxiliary loss keeping that routing balanced.
The price isn't accuracy — it's engineering: all experts must fit in distributed memory, and tokens must be shuttled to the right device.
Reach for MoE when raw capacity matters more than serving simplicity; skip it when you can't amortize the memory and communication overhead.

questions.prompt: In an MoE layer with top-2 routing out of 8 experts, how many experts actually process a given token?
options: All 8
Only 2
Only 1
A random number each time
questions.explanation: Top-k routing with k=2 means the gate scores all 8 experts and sends the token only to the 2 highest-scoring ones — the other 6 do zero work for that token. That's exactly where MoE's compute savings come from.

questions.prompt: Why do MoE models need an auxiliary 'load-balancing' loss during training?
options: To make the model's output more creative
To stop the router from sending most tokens to just one or two favorite experts, leaving the rest undertrained
To reduce the total number of parameters
To speed up tokenization
questions.explanation: Without a balancing signal, gradient descent tends to funnel tokens to whichever experts got a head start — a feedback loop called router/expert collapse. The auxiliary loss penalizes imbalance so every expert gets trained and used.

questions.prompt: A Mixtral-style MoE model has far more total parameters than a same-active-compute dense model. What's the main operational cost of that extra capacity?
options: Slower token generation because every expert runs on every token
Higher memory requirements, since all experts must stay resident even though only a few are used per token
It can no longer be fine-tuned
It always produces lower-quality output
questions.explanation: MoE saves compute, not memory — every expert's weights must sit in GPU memory (or be reachable across a cluster) even though a given token only activates a couple of them. That's why MoE serving is memory- and communication-heavy, not compute-heavy.

posts.title: The Missing Map of the Sky: Claude Fills GALEX's Gaps
posts.subtitle: A swarm of agents stitched a decade-old UV survey gap into one self-correcting map
posts.summary: Astrophysicist Brice Ménard used Claude Science to stitch NASA's GALEX ultraviolet survey (which deliberately skipped a third of the sky to protect its detectors) with other missions, then trained an inpainting model to fill the gap with per-pixel confidence estimates. Claude's agents also caught and fixed their own calibration mistake across 38,000 observations.

slides.title: A Third of the UV Sky Had No Data — For Over a Decade
slides.body: NASA's GALEX mission mapped about two-thirds of the sky in ultraviolet between 2003 and 2013. The rest sat blank, flagged as too risky to shoot.
bullets: GALEX ran 38,000 separate observations between 2003-2013
It deliberately skipped the Milky Way's plane and regions near bright stars
Filling the gap by hand needed weeks of pixel-level calibration — so it never got done

slides.title: Why Nobody Finished the Job
slides.body: Ultraviolet light is absorbed by Earth's atmosphere, so it can only be observed from space — and space telescopes have fragile detectors.
bullets: Bright stars can saturate or damage a UV detector, so GALEX's team programmed it to avoid them entirely
Other missions (Swift, South Korea's FIMS/SPEAR, Europe's TD-1) covered scraps of the gap, but in different resolutions and calibrations
Merging incompatible instruments onto one coordinate grid is exactly the kind of tedious, error-prone work that stays a backlog item forever

slides.title: Claude Science Ran the Pipeline as a Swarm of Agents
slides.body: Ménard gave high-level direction; many Claude agents executed the pipeline in parallel.
bullets: Collect: agents found and downloaded tens of thousands of public GALEX images plus Swift and FIMS/SPEAR data
Clean: agents removed stellar glare around bright stars so faint UV signal underneath could be measured
Merge: cross-calibrated every instrument, resampled to one resolution, and placed them on a shared coordinate system
Fill: trained an inpainting model on the relationship between UV and the visible/infrared/radio data available everywhere, then applied it to the unobserved third with per-pixel confidence scores

slides.title: When the Map Was Wrong, Claude Found Its Own Mistake
slides.body: Validation wasn't just a final check — it caught a real error mid-pipeline.
bullets: To validate, Claude hid patches of known UV data, predicted them blind, and compared — after several refinement rounds, predictions landed within about 10% of real measurements
But circular artifacts from residual atmospheric glow in individual GALEX pointings slipped past two full rounds of automated agent review
Once Ménard flagged the pattern, Claude re-processed and corrected all 38,000 observations in a few hours

slides.title: Where This Map Should Make You Cautious
slides.body: A map that's one-third inferred is genuinely useful — but only if you remember which third.
bullets: About a third of the final map, including much of the galactic plane, is predicted by the model, not directly observed by any telescope
Inpainting assumes UV brightness correlates with visible/infrared/radio data — it will quietly fail on any genuinely novel UV source that breaks that correlation
Two rounds of autonomous agent review missed the glow artifacts; it took a human scientist's eye to catch the pattern — autonomous validation isn't foolproof yet

slides.title: What Each Data Source Contributed
Why This Matters
slides.body: This isn't a toy demo — it's a public scientific resource with its uncertainty labeled.
bullets: Every pixel in the final map is tagged 'measured' or 'predicted,' with an uncertainty estimate attached
The map adds UV brightness estimates for more than 100 million individual stars, inferred from Gaia's visible-light data
It's public at menard.pha.jhu.edu/uvmap, covering far-UV (154nm) and near-UV (232nm), and shows real structures: dust clouds, supernova gas-bubble rings, and the Magellanic Clouds
The workflow — a scientist directs, agents execute and iterate, a human catches the one systematic error agents missed — is the template, not the astronomy itself

questions.prompt: Why did GALEX deliberately skip parts of the sky during its 2003-2013 survey?
options: Funding ran out before the mission finished
To protect its detectors from bright stars
Those regions already had complete UV data from other missions
Cloud cover on Earth blocked those observations
questions.explanation: GALEX's detectors could be saturated or damaged by intense UV light, so the mission was programmed to avoid bright-star regions and the Milky Way's plane entirely.

questions.prompt: How did Claude validate its gap-filling predictions before trusting them?
options: It compared results to a panel of astronomers' rankings
It hid patches of already-measured UV data, predicted them blind, and checked the error
It relied solely on visual inspection of the final image
It trained once and shipped without further checking
questions.explanation: Claude held out known UV regions, predicted them with the same inpainting model used for the real gap, and iterated until predictions came within about 10% of the real measurements.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of the final all-sky UV map is predicted rather than directly observed?
options: About 5%
About one-third
About two-thirds
About 90%
questions.explanation: Roughly a third of the map — including most of the galactic plane — is inferred by the inpainting model rather than measured by a telescope, and each pixel is explicitly labeled as measured or predicted.

posts.title: Claude Code Review Goes GA: 3x Faster, Three Depth Settings
posts.subtitle: Automatic review on every pull request, tunable from Quick to Deep
posts.summary: Claude Code Review exited research preview on October 15, 2026, and is now on by default for Claude Team and Enterprise organizations. Reviews run about 3x faster than in preview (6-10 minutes versus ~20), admins can tune depth per repository, and developers get automatic reviews on new PRs with zero configuration.

slides.title: Code Review Ships to Every Pull Request — Automatically
slides.body: What was a research preview is now a standing part of the PR workflow for Claude Team and Enterprise orgs.
bullets: Exited research preview on October 15, 2026
Triggers automatically on every new pull request once enabled — zero configuration for developers
Anthropic runs it on its own pull requests before shipping features

slides.title: Preview Was Accurate But Too Slow to Trust in CI
slides.body: A 20-minute review can't realistically gate a merge — by the time it finishes, the team has already moved on.
bullets: Original preview reviews took roughly 20 minutes per PR
Teams wanted reviews fast enough to actually block a merge, not just arrive as a slow, advisory afterthought
Too many low-value comments bury the one bug that actually matters

slides.title: Three Knobs: Quick, Standard, Deep
slides.body: Instead of one fixed review mode, admins choose depth per repository.
bullets: Quick — fastest, cheapest pass, for lower-stakes repos
Standard — the default, balances speed and thoroughness
Deep — full architectural review for high-stakes repos, trading speed for scrutiny
Setup is entirely admin-side: install the GitHub App, enable Code Review, pick a depth per repo — developers change nothing

slides.title: What Actually Changed Under the Hood
slides.body: The speedup wasn't just infrastructure — the review format itself got tighter.
bullets: Reviews now typically finish in about 6-10 minutes, down from roughly 20 — close to a 3x speedup
Findings are now structured as problem, trigger condition, and fix — cutting the noise of low-value comments
Anthropic dogfoods Code Review on its own pull requests as part of validating each change

slides.title: Same PR, Three Different Depths
slides.body: The depth setting changes what kind of review a given pull request gets, not just how long it takes.
bullets: Quick depth on a small docs-only PR: a fast pass that flags only clear, obvious issues
Standard depth on a typical feature PR: catches logic bugs and edge cases within the normal 6-10 minute window
Deep depth on a PR touching auth or billing code: slower, broader architectural scrutiny — reserved deliberately for high-stakes changes, not run by default everywhere

slides.title: Where It Still Falls Short
slides.body: GA doesn't mean solved — there are real gaps worth knowing about before you lean on it.
bullets: No published accuracy or bug-catch-rate benchmark — the headline metric at GA is speed, not precision
Only available to Claude Team and Enterprise plans, not Pro or free tiers
Deep mode's extra scrutiny costs time, so teams must deliberately opt specific repos into it rather than getting it everywhere automatically

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.body: GA status plus a 3x speedup is what turns a review tool from an experiment into infrastructure.
bullets: The speed cut makes it realistic to let Code Review actually gate a merge instead of arriving after the fact
Eligible Enterprise orgs can claim at least $10,000 in Code Review credits through January 15, 2027
No bug-catch-rate benchmark has been published yet, so it's still worth pairing with human review rather than replacing it outright

posts.title: Consistent Hashing: Scaling Without a Full Reshuffle
posts.subtitle: Why adding one node shouldn't move 80% of your keys
posts.summary: Plain hash(key) % N remaps most keys every time a node joins or leaves a cluster. Consistent hashing fixes this by placing nodes and keys on the same ring so only a local neighborhood of keys moves — and virtual nodes keep that movement evenly spread across the real machines.

slides.title: Add One More Node Without Reshuffling Everything
slides.body: Consistent hashing is the technique behind scaling caches and databases without a cache-miss storm every time the cluster changes size.
bullets: Naive hash(key) % N remaps almost every key when N changes
Consistent hashing keeps roughly 1/N of keys moving when a node joins or leaves
Used in DynamoDB, Cassandra, memcached clients, CDNs, and load balancers

slides.title: Why hash(key) % N Breaks at Scale
slides.body: The modulo operation ties every key's owner directly to the total node count — so the moment that count changes, almost nothing stays put.
bullets: Changing N from 4 to 5 nodes relocates roughly (N-1)/N of all keys — about 80% churn
Every node addition or removal triggers a mass cache-miss storm across the whole cluster
At scale, with hundreds of shards, this makes routine horizontal scaling operationally painful

slides.title: Put Nodes and Keys on the Same Ring
slides.body: Instead of hashing keys against a count, hash both nodes and keys onto one fixed circular space.
bullets: Hash both server IDs and keys onto a fixed ring, e.g. the range 0 to 2^32-1
A key belongs to the first node found clockwise from its position on the ring
Adding a node only steals keys from its immediate clockwise neighbor — not from every other node in the cluster

slides.title: Virtual Nodes Fix the Lumpy-Ring Problem
slides.body: A handful of physical nodes placed directly on the ring creates uneven arcs — some nodes end up owning far more keys than others.
bullets: Fix: hash each physical node into 100-200 virtual points scattered around the ring, instead of just one
Load evens out because the uneven-arc variance averages away across many virtual positions per real node
This is exactly what Cassandra and DynamoDB both do in production to keep load balanced

slides.title: Worked Example: 4 Nodes Become 5
slides.body: A ring holding nodes A, B, C, D at fixed hash positions, with keys assigned clockwise.
bullets: Adding node E inserts it onto the ring between C and D
Only the keys that previously mapped to D and fall before E's new position move to E — roughly 1/5 of total keys
Every other node's keys (A, B, C, and D's remaining keys) are completely untouched by the change

slides.title: Key Movement: Mod-N vs. Consistent Hashing

rows: No — only the new node's ring neighbor

slides.title: When It's Overkill or Risky
slides.body: Consistent hashing solves a real problem, but it's not free complexity you want everywhere.
bullets: For a fixed, rarely-resized cluster, plain mod-N hashing is simpler and perfectly fine — don't add ring complexity you don't need
Without virtual nodes, a small number of physical nodes can still land unevenly on the ring and get a lumpy load distribution
Consistent hashing alone doesn't handle replication — systems like DynamoDB add a replication factor on top, storing each key on the next R nodes clockwise

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.body: The core idea generalizes far beyond caches — it's the same trick behind sharding and request routing at scale.
bullets: Core idea: map nodes and keys onto the same ring so only a local neighborhood of keys moves when membership changes
Virtual nodes are what actually make load balanced in real production systems — not the ring alone
In use today in DynamoDB, Cassandra, Riak, and many CDN and load-balancer designs
Interview tip: always mention virtual nodes — that's almost always the follow-up question after you describe the basic ring

questions.prompt: With plain hash(key) % N, what happens when a cluster goes from 4 nodes to 5?
options: No keys move
About 20% of keys move
About 80% of keys move
Exactly one key moves
questions.explanation: Mod-N hashing ties every key's owner to the total node count N, so changing N remaps roughly (N-1)/N of all keys — about 80% churn going from 4 to 5 nodes.

questions.prompt: What problem do 'virtual nodes' solve in a consistent hashing scheme?
options: They encrypt data on the ring
They replace the need for a hash function
They even out load when a small number of physical nodes land unevenly on the ring
They eliminate the need for a hash ring entirely
questions.explanation: A few physical nodes placed directly on the ring can create uneven arcs. Hashing each physical node into 100-200 virtual positions averages that variance away, balancing load across real machines.

questions.prompt: When node E is inserted onto the ring between nodes C and D, which keys move to E?
options: Every key in the system
Only the keys that previously belonged to D and now fall before E's position
A random 50% sample of all keys
No keys move — only metadata changes
questions.explanation: Only the keys in the arc between C and E's new position — previously owned by D — move to E. Every other node's keys are untouched, which is the whole point of consistent hashing.

posts.title: OpenGCUA: Letting the Model Run Your Whole Computer
posts.subtitle: Code execution plus harness-to-model decision transfer cuts agent steps 53%
posts.summary: OpenGCUA, an open stack from Alibaba's Tongyi-MAI team, lets agents write code instead of clicking one GUI element at a time, and moves key decisions from a fixed harness into the model itself. Across eight frontier models on OSWorld-v2, mean partial score rose from 45.3 to 64.9 while steps per task fell 53%.

slides.title: Why Can't an Agent Just Use a Whole Computer?
slides.body: Frontier computer-use agents like GPT-6 Astra are closed systems. A new open stack, OpenGCUA, tries to show what makes them work — and open-sources the whole pipeline.

slides.title: GUI-Only Agents Hardcode Three Decisions
slides.body: Most computer-use agents fix the same three choices inside the harness, not the model.
bullets: What to observe: take a fresh screenshot after every single action, even trivial ones
How to act: one GUI click, type, or scroll per step — no branching, no loops
How to track progress: no persistent plan across a long task

slides.title: Two Ideas: Code Execution + Decision Transfer
slides.body: OpenGCUA's core move is handing those three decisions to the model instead of the scaffold.
bullets: Code execution: the model writes a Python program per step that mixes accessibility-tree reads, app APIs, shell commands, and GUI clicks — with loops and branches
Harness-to-model decision transfer: the model decides when it actually needs a screenshot, instead of taking one every step
Before each program it writes an <intent> statement and keeps a running todo list, so planning survives across dozens of steps

slides.title: The Numbers: Fewer Steps, Higher Scores
slides.body: Measured on the OSWorld-v2 offline benchmark across eight frontier models (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen3.8-Max, Qwen3.8-Flash, Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash).

slides.title: Worked Example: Reorganizing 200 Files
slides.body: Imagine the task is 'sort these 200 downloaded files into folders by date modified.'
bullets: GUI-only agent: screenshot, click file, read date, drag to folder, screenshot again — repeated 200 times, burning hundreds of steps
OpenGCUA agent: writes one short script that reads all file metadata via the accessibility API and loops to move each file, taking a screenshot only to confirm the result
The paper reports code execution alone adds +6.1 points and cuts steps 14.8% versus GUI+CLI access, averaged over three models

slides.title: Weaker Models Gain the Most — and Limits Remain
slides.body: The gains aren't evenly spread, and the real-device story is still early.
bullets: GLM-5.3-Flash improved +35.2 points and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash +29.8 — code execution narrows the gap between strong and weak models more than it widens it
On four real macOS tasks, Qwen3.8-Max burned 19.4x the reasoning tokens of GPT-6 Astra and still finished only 3 of 4 tasks, versus 4 of 4 for GPT-6 Astra
The real-device harness and cross-device SDK are both marked 'preliminary' — this is a research preview, not a production agent

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.body: OpenGCUA is a case for an architectural idea, not just a leaderboard entry.
bullets: Letting models write code to interact with a computer, instead of clicking through a fixed GUI loop, is a more general interface than screenshot-and-click
Full trajectories for all eight evaluated models are public, so anyone can study why one model times out or loops where another doesn't
Released under Apache-2.0 with code, prompts, and eval trajectories — a rare fully-open look at a computer-use stack

questions.prompt: What are the two core ideas behind OpenGCUA?
options: A bigger model and more training data
Code execution and harness-to-model decision transfer
A faster screenshot renderer and a new GUI library
Reinforcement learning from human feedback on clicks
questions.explanation: OpenGCUA's headline contribution is letting the model write code to act (instead of one GUI click per step) and moving decisions like 'when to look at the screen' from the fixed harness into the model.

questions.prompt: On the OSWorld-v2 offline benchmark, what happened to steps-per-task under OpenGCUA?
options: They roughly doubled
They stayed the same but accuracy rose
They fell by about 53% on average, alongside a +19.6 point score gain
They fell only for the single strongest model
questions.explanation: Across eight frontier models, mean partial score rose from 45.3 to 64.9 while steps per task dropped 53% on average — fewer, more effective actions per task.

questions.prompt: Which models benefited most from the OpenGCUA approach?
options: The strongest models got relatively stronger, widening the gap
All models gained identically
Weaker models like GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash gained the most, shrinking the gap between strongest and weakest
Only closed frontier models like GPT-6 Astra improved
questions.explanation: The strongest-to-weakest score gap shrank from 39.1 to 18.0 points, driven by large gains for weaker models — code execution seems to compensate for weaker raw reasoning.

posts.title: Scion: Why Anthropic Replaced Git in Its Own Monorepo
posts.subtitle: Always-online clients, a server that owns history, and ~200x less infrastructure
posts.summary: Anthropic migrated its entire monorepo off git to an in-house system called Scion, built around always-online clients and a server that owns history, blame, and merges. The result: about 200x less infrastructure than the old git mirror fleet and checkouts that take seconds instead of minutes.

slides.title: Why Anthropic Stopped Using Git
slides.body: Claude-written code grew Anthropic's monorepo faster than git's distributed, offline-first design could handle — so they built a replacement: Scion.

slides.title: Git Wasn't Built for an Always-Online Fleet of Agents
slides.body: Daily merged changes rose from about 2,500 in May 2026 to over 30,000 by September — roughly 12x in four months.
bullets: Main branch history is nearly 100GB; a compressed working copy alone is over 25GB
About 25 million checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer machines, agent sandboxes, and research jobs
A naive git fetch model at that volume implies over 600 petabytes of traffic a day
Several hundred internal git mirrors were running at peak just to keep up, and they kept drifting from the tip of main

slides.title: Scion: Assume the Client Is Always Online
slides.body: Instead of git's offline-first model where every clone holds the full history, Scion flips the assumption.
bullets: Clients fetch data on demand from a reachable server rather than syncing a full copy
The server owns history, blame, commits, merges, and rebases; the client just keeps a bounded local cache
'Source control as an API': CI jobs and bisect/revert tools can query history or run operations with no local repository at all
Commits happen server-side with no push step, so cost scales with the size of the change, not the size of the repo

slides.title: Three Tiers, One Protocol
slides.body: Scion's data model is a changeset in a write-ahead log, not a git-style tree snapshot.
bullets: A changeset lists only the files changed relative to its first parent, with content-addressed pointers to compressed blobs
scion-daemon runs per node for local jobs; scion-cache runs per region and streams objects from memory; scion-server is authoritative, backed by Spanner and cloud storage
Ref updates (like moving 'main') are a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row, decoupled from changeset creation
Design borrows from Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling/Mononoke, whose Bonsai data model directly influenced Scion's changesets

slides.title: Git Mirror Fleet vs. Scion
Worked Example: A Bisect Job With No Checkout
slides.body: An automated bisect pipeline needs to find which of 10,000 commits introduced a regression.
bullets: On git, that means cloning or fetching enough history locally to walk the commit graph, then checking out candidate commits one by one
On Scion, the bisect tool calls the history API directly — reading ancestry and blame as RPCs — and only materializes a sparse working copy for the final candidate it needs to actually run
Anthropic also had Claude Mythos Preview rewrite the hand-built git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline itself, cutting its memory use 20x and roughly quadrupling its speed

slides.title: Not a General Git Replacement
slides.body: Anthropic is explicit that Scion only pays off at a specific kind of scale.
bullets: It only makes sense for enormous monorepos with heavy always-online CI and agent traffic — not a typical multi-repo team's workflow
Migrating took a dedicated team of seven people about five months, plus building a matching code review tool (Antique), code search, and a new IAM system alongside it
Global merge locks don't fit agent-scale commit rates, so Scion leans on post-merge and pre-deploy testing instead — occasional conflicts slip through and get fixed after the fact
Anthropic is still working with GitHub, GitLab, and the open-source community on whether any of these ideas (server-side RPCs, scalable server architectures) can go mainstream

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.body: Scion is a concrete data point on what breaks when AI agents, not just humans, become your main committers.
bullets: Git's core assumption — every client eventually holds a full, offline copy of history — stops scaling once checkouts are driven by thousands of always-online CI jobs and agent sandboxes
Treating source control as a queryable API, not just a sync protocol, let Anthropic cut infrastructure roughly 200x versus its old mirror fleet
It's a preview of an infrastructure problem other large AI labs and engineering orgs will likely hit as agentic coding volume grows

questions.prompt: What's the central design shift Scion makes versus git?
options: Scion stores more data on each client than git does
Scion assumes clients are always online and fetch on demand, while the server owns history, blame, and merges
Scion removes the need for a server entirely
Scion only works for single-file repositories
questions.explanation: Git is distributed and offline-first: every clone eventually holds a full copy. Scion assumes clients are always connected, so they fetch what they need on demand while the server stays authoritative over history.

questions.prompt: What triggered Anthropic to build Scion in the first place?
options: A security vulnerability discovered in git
A licensing dispute with GitHub
Daily merged changes grew roughly 12x in four months, overwhelming git-based infrastructure
A decision to open-source all internal tooling
questions.explanation: Daily merged changes rose from about 2,500 in May 2026 to over 30,000 by September, driven largely by AI-assisted coding — git's offline-first design and the surrounding mirror fleet couldn't keep up.

questions.prompt: According to Anthropic, when does Scion's approach make sense?
options: For any team using git, regardless of size
Only for small personal projects
Only for enormous monorepos with heavy always-online CI and agent traffic — not a general git replacement
Only for repositories with no CI pipeline
questions.explanation: Anthropic is explicit that Scion isn't a general-purpose git replacement — it only pays off at a scale where hundreds of git mirrors and tens of millions of daily checkouts were already straining, and it requires building matching review, search, and CI tooling.

posts.title: Test-Time Compute: Making a Model Smarter Without Retraining It
posts.subtitle: Why some LLMs get better answers by thinking longer, not by getting bigger
posts.summary: Test-time compute means spending extra inference-time work — longer reasoning chains, multiple sampled candidates, or search over partial solutions — to get a better answer from the same trained model. It trades latency and cost for accuracy, and it's the idea behind 'thinking budgets' and reasoning-tuned models.

slides.title: Spend More Compute at Answer Time, Not Just Training Time
slides.body: For years, 'make the model better' meant train a bigger one. Test-time compute asks a different question: what if the same model could get smarter just by working harder on a single question?

slides.title: Two Different Knobs to Turn
slides.body: Train-time scaling and test-time scaling solve the same problem in opposite ways.
bullets: Train-time scaling: bigger model, more data, more training compute — expensive, paid once, fixed after deployment
Test-time compute: same trained model, more work per query at inference — cheap to turn on or off per request, paid every time you use it
You can combine both: a smaller, cheaper model with heavy test-time compute can match a much larger model on hard problems

slides.title: The Mechanisms: Sequential and Parallel
slides.body: Test-time compute isn't one technique — it's a family of them, falling into two families.
bullets: Sequential: generate a longer chain-of-thought (extended 'thinking' tokens) before answering, so the model reasons step-by-step instead of jumping straight to an answer
Parallel: sample N independent answers and combine them — self-consistency takes a majority vote; best-of-N uses a verifier or reward model to pick the strongest candidate
Search: tree-of-thought / Monte Carlo methods branch over partial solutions and prune bad paths instead of committing to one linear chain
Iterative refinement: generate a draft, critique it, then revise — repeating the loop until the critique has nothing left to flag

slides.title: Worked Example: A Tricky Word Problem
slides.body: Ask a model: 'A train leaves at 2:15 and arrives at 5:05 after a 20-minute stop. How long was it actually moving?'
bullets: Zero extra compute: the model pattern-matches to 'end minus start' and answers 2h 50m — wrong, because it forgot to subtract the stop
With extended thinking: the model works through the subtraction step by step, catches the stop, and answers 2h 30m
With best-of-8 sampling: even if 3 of 8 samples make the same mistake, majority vote or a verifier surfaces the 5 correct answers
Both routes spend more inference compute on the same question to fix the same class of error

slides.title: Train-Time vs. Test-Time Scaling
When It's a Waste of Tokens
slides.body: Extra compute isn't free, and it doesn't help everywhere.
bullets: Simple factual lookups ('what's the capital of Peru?') get no benefit — there's nothing to reason through, so you just pay more latency and cost
Returns diminish: doubling the thinking budget rarely doubles accuracy, and past a point extra tokens just restate the same reasoning
Heavy search with a learned verifier can be gamed — the model finds answers that fool the verifier rather than ones that are actually correct ('reward hacking')
User-facing products with tight latency budgets (autocomplete, voice assistants) often can't afford multi-second 'thinking' pauses

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.body: Test-time compute reframes 'how smart is this model' as a dial, not a fixed property.
bullets: It's why products now expose a 'thinking budget' or reasoning-effort setting instead of one fixed quality level per model
It lets teams route easy queries to cheap, fast, low-compute answers and reserve expensive reasoning for the queries that actually need it
The core tradeoff to remember: more test-time compute buys accuracy on hard problems at the direct cost of latency and tokens — spend it where the problem is actually hard

questions.prompt: What is test-time compute, in one sentence?
options: Training a larger model on more data
Spending extra inference-time work — like longer reasoning or multiple sampled answers — to improve a response from an already-trained model
A method for compressing model weights after training
A benchmark for measuring GPU throughput
questions.explanation: Test-time compute is about spending more computation when answering a specific query — longer chains of thought, more sampled candidates, or search — rather than changing the model's weights or training process.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of 'parallel' test-time compute?
options: Generating one long chain-of-thought before answering
Sampling N independent answers and picking the best via majority vote or a verifier
Training the model for more epochs
Quantizing the model to 4-bit weights
questions.explanation: Parallel test-time compute means generating multiple independent candidate answers at once and combining them (self-consistency voting, or best-of-N with a verifier) — as opposed to sequential methods that extend a single reasoning chain.

questions.prompt: When does test-time compute tend to be a poor investment?
options: On genuinely hard multi-step reasoning problems
When accuracy matters more than latency
On simple factual lookups with no reasoning required, or under tight latency budgets
When the model has a long context window
questions.explanation: Extra thinking or sampling doesn't help when there's nothing to reason through — a simple factual query gains nothing from it, and it still costs extra tokens and latency, which is especially costly for latency-sensitive products.

posts.title: Hybrid Search: Fusing Keyword and Vector Retrieval
posts.subtitle: Why production RAG systems run BM25 and embeddings side by side instead of picking one.
posts.summary: Hybrid search runs a sparse keyword method like BM25 alongside dense vector embeddings, then fuses the two ranked lists into one — because each catches failures the other misses. Vector search finds paraphrases and lets 'cheap car' match 'affordable vehicle'; BM25 finds the exact SKU or error code that an embedding happily looks past.

slides.title: Why RAG Needs Two Search Engines, Not One
slides.body: Semantic (vector) search and classic keyword search each have blind spots that the other doesn't.
bullets: Vector search embeds queries and documents into the same space and ranks by cosine/dot-product similarity
BM25 is a decades-old sparse keyword scoring function that ranks by term frequency, weighted by how rare that term is
Hybrid search runs both and merges the results — it isn't an either/or choice

slides.title: Where Each Method Fails Alone
slides.body: The two failure modes are almost opposite, which is exactly why combining them works.
bullets: Pure vector search: a query for an exact error code or part number can retrieve semantically 'similar' but wrong documents, because embeddings blur exact tokens
Pure BM25: a query for 'inexpensive transportation' won't match a document that only says 'cheap car', because there's no shared literal token
Acronyms, product SKUs, names, and numbers are classic vector-search blind spots; paraphrase and intent are classic BM25 blind spots

slides.title: The Mechanism: Two Ranked Lists, One Fused Score
slides.body: Hybrid search doesn't average raw scores — BM25 and cosine similarity live on incomparable scales. It fuses rankings instead.
bullets: Each retriever (BM25, vector) independently returns its own top-k ranked list for the same query
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) scores each document by summing 1/(rank + k) across every list it appears in — a document ranked highly by both methods wins
A tunable weight can bias the fusion toward one retriever when a domain favors it — e.g. more keyword weight for legal/code search, more vector weight for conversational FAQ

slides.title: Where It Sits in a RAG Pipeline
slides.body: Hybrid retrieval is typically the first of two retrieval stages, not the last.
bullets: Stage 1 (hybrid retrieval): BM25 + vector search each pull dozens of candidates cheaply from the full corpus
Stage 2 (reranking): a smaller cross-encoder model re-scores just those candidates against the query for precision, since cross-encoders are too slow to run over an entire corpus
The LLM only ever sees the final top-k (often 3-10) chunks that survive both stages

slides.title: Worked Example: An Internal Support Bot
slides.body: A query like "why does invoice INV-88213 show as void" needs both halves.
bullets: Vector search alone: ranks documents about 'why invoices get cancelled' highly, but the literal invoice ID 'INV-88213' may not surface the one ticket that mentions it, since embeddings don't preserve exact IDs well
BM25 alone: finds every document containing the literal string 'INV-88213' instantly, but ranks a generic FAQ about voided invoices (which never uses that exact phrase) far too low
Hybrid + RRF: the ticket mentioning the exact ID ranks near the top from BM25, the conceptually relevant FAQ ranks near the top from vector search — fusion surfaces both

slides.title: BM25 vs. Vector vs. Hybrid

rows: Inverted index only — no embedding model needed
Both of the above, plus a fusion step

slides.title: When Hybrid Isn't Worth the Extra Piece
slides.body: Hybrid search adds a second retrieval system and a fusion step to maintain — that cost has to earn its keep.
bullets: Skip it for small, tightly-scoped corpora (a few hundred FAQ entries) where either method alone already finds everything
Skip it if queries are purely conversational with no IDs, codes, or exact terms ever involved — vector search alone may be enough
Don't skip the reranking stage and expect fusion alone to fix ordering — RRF improves recall of candidates, a cross-encoder improves final precision
Tune the fusion weight per domain: code/log search usually wants more BM25 weight, open-ended Q&A usually wants more vector weight

questions.prompt: Why doesn't hybrid search just average the raw BM25 score and the cosine similarity score?
options: Averaging would be too slow to compute
The two scores live on incomparable scales, so hybrid search fuses the rankings (e.g. via Reciprocal Rank Fusion) instead of the raw scores
BM25 doesn't produce a numeric score
Cosine similarity can't be computed for text
questions.explanation: BM25 and cosine similarity aren't on the same scale or distribution, so naively averaging them is meaningless — rank-based fusion methods like RRF sidestep that by combining positions in each ranked list instead.

questions.prompt: What's a classic failure mode of pure vector (embedding) search?
options: It's always slower than BM25
It struggles with exact tokens like IDs, SKUs, or error codes because embeddings blur literal strings into semantic space
It can't handle long documents
It requires no index at all
questions.explanation: Embeddings are great at capturing meaning and paraphrase, but they compress exact tokens into a continuous space, which makes exact-match lookups like part numbers or error codes unreliable.

questions.prompt: In a typical two-stage RAG retrieval pipeline, what does the reranking stage add that hybrid retrieval alone doesn't?
options: It replaces the need for any retrieval at all
It fetches documents from a second corpus
It re-scores a small candidate set with a more precise (but slower) cross-encoder model, improving final ordering before the LLM sees the chunks
It deletes irrelevant documents from the database
questions.explanation: Cross-encoders are far more accurate at judging query-document relevance than BM25 or cosine similarity, but too slow to run over an entire corpus — so they only rerank the candidates hybrid retrieval already narrowed down.

posts.title: Context Engineering: Curating What the Model Sees
posts.subtitle: Prompt engineering wrote one instruction well; context engineering decides what fills the whole window, every turn.
posts.summary: Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what fills an LLM's limited context window at every step — not just how one prompt is worded. As agents run longer and call more tools, treating context as a scarce, curatable resource (via retrieval, compaction, and sub-agents) becomes the difference between an agent that stays sharp and one that drowns in its own history.

slides.title: Prompt Engineering Solved One Call. This Solves the Whole Run.
slides.body: A single well-worded prompt doesn't help once an agent is 40 tool calls deep. Context engineering is the ongoing job of deciding exactly what fills the window at each step.
bullets: Prompt engineering: craft the wording of one instruction
Context engineering: curate everything else — tools, retrieved data, message history, prior results — across an entire session
Anthropic frames it as the direct successor discipline as agents got longer-running

slides.title: Context Rot: More Tokens, Worse Recall
slides.body: Every token a model reads has to be related to every other token — attention is pairwise, so cost grows roughly with the square of context length (n²).
bullets: Recall accuracy measurably drops as token count grows — across all model families, just to different degrees — a pattern Anthropic calls 'context rot'
Context is a finite, diminishing-returns resource, not a free bucket to dump everything into
The guiding principle: find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that makes the right outcome likely

slides.title: Three Techniques for Long-Running Agents
slides.body: Once a task runs long enough to threaten the window, three complementary techniques keep context lean.
bullets: Compaction — summarize a near-full window and restart with the summary; Claude Code keeps the compressed summary plus its 5 most recently accessed files
Structured note-taking — the agent writes progress to an external file (a NOTES.md or to-do list) and reads it back later instead of re-deriving state
Sub-agents — a specialized agent explores in its own clean context (burning tens of thousands of tokens if needed) and hands back only a condensed 1,000-2,000 token summary

slides.title: Retrieval: Load It Now, or Load It Just-in-Time?
slides.body: Where data enters the context window is itself a design decision.
bullets: Pre-retrieval: embed and fetch relevant chunks before inference — fast, but front-loads tokens the model might not need
Just-in-time: keep lightweight references (file paths, query strings) and let the agent pull data with a tool only when it's actually needed
Claude Code runs a hybrid: it drops CLAUDE.md into context upfront, then uses glob/grep plus head/tail to explore large files on demand instead of loading them whole

slides.title: 1,234 Steps of Pokémon Without Losing the Plot
slides.body: Anthropic's long-horizon agent demo tracked a multi-hour Pokémon playthrough using structured notes instead of cramming the whole history into context.
bullets: The agent logged concrete progress externally — e.g. 'Pikachu: level 8 of a target of 10' — and re-read that note on later turns
Over 1,234 steps, nothing about the running state had to survive inside the live context window itself
Same pattern as a to-do list: the context window holds the current step, the file holds everything that came before

slides.title: Prompt Engineering vs. Context Engineering

rows: Everything that fills the window: tools, history, retrieved data
Context rot — diluted attention, slower and less accurate outputs

slides.title: When Curation Beats Accumulation
slides.body: Anthropic's own advice: 'do the simplest thing that works' — escalate only when you can show the window is actually straining.
bullets: Don't reach for compaction or sub-agents on short tasks — that's overhead a simple prompt doesn't need
Compaction fits long back-and-forth conversation; note-taking fits iterative work with clear milestones; sub-agents fit parallel research
Tune compaction for recall first, precision second — losing a needed detail is worse than keeping one extra
A bloated, overlapping toolset burns context and causes bad tool choices just as much as a messy prompt does

questions.prompt: What does Anthropic mean by "context rot"?
options: Context windows shrinking over model updates
Recall accuracy degrading as the number of tokens in context grows
Tool definitions becoming outdated
Training data becoming stale
questions.explanation: Context rot describes a measurable drop in recall accuracy as token count grows — true across model families to varying degrees, which is why dumping everything into context isn't actually 'safer'.

questions.prompt: Why do sub-agents help with context engineering?
options: They give the model more parameters to work with
They let specialized agents explore in a clean context and return only a condensed summary (often 1,000-2,000 tokens) to the lead agent
They skip the need for a system prompt entirely
They run the model at a lower temperature
questions.explanation: A sub-agent can burn tens of thousands of tokens exploring a problem in its own window, but the lead agent only ever sees the condensed result — keeping the main context lean.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between pre-retrieval and just-in-time retrieval?
options: Pre-retrieval only works with images
Pre-retrieval loads relevant context before inference; just-in-time keeps lightweight references and loads data with a tool only when needed
Just-in-time retrieval is always slower
Pre-retrieval requires no embeddings
questions.explanation: Pre-retrieval front-loads tokens for speed; just-in-time (e.g. Claude Code's use of glob/grep/head/tail) trades a little latency for only ever loading what's actually needed.

posts.title: OSS Scanner: Anthropic Turns Claude Loose on Open-Source Bugs
posts.subtitle: A free, opt-in vulnerability hunter that already turned 72 of 74 reports into real wolfSSL fixes.
posts.summary: Anthropic launched OSS Scanner, a free opt-in service that runs its strongest Claude models against open-source codebases to find vulnerabilities, bisect when they were introduced, and draft candidate patches — with no human review before a report reaches maintainers. Early validation found 88% of a penetration-tester-checked sample were real, disclosure-worthy bugs.

slides.title: Claude Goes Hunting for Bugs in Your Dependencies
slides.body: On October 8, 2026, Anthropic's Frontier Red Team launched OSS Scanner: a free, opt-in service that points its strongest models at open-source codebases and reports what it finds.
bullets: No fee, no fuzzing harness to write — maintainers just opt in
Modeled on Google's OSS-Fuzz, but swaps fuzzers for language-model reasoning

slides.title: Most Open-Source Security Runs on Volunteer Hours
slides.body: Critical infrastructure software — TLS libraries, parsers, compression codecs — is often maintained by a handful of volunteers with no dedicated security budget.
bullets: Fuzzing tools like OSS-Fuzz are effective but only catch bugs that crash on malformed input, not logic or protocol-level flaws
Manual security audits of C/C++ codebases are expensive and rare outside well-funded projects
Anthropic frames the gap plainly: defenders need the same frontier capability attackers already have access to

slides.title: The Service: Scan, Explain, Bisect, Patch
slides.body: OSS Scanner runs periodic scans of enrolled projects using Anthropic's strongest models, including Claude Mythos, at no cost to the project.
bullets: Each report ships a self-contained reproducer — code that triggers the bug, not just a description of it
Where possible, the report bisects history to show the exact commit that introduced the vulnerability
A candidate patch is attached when the model can produce one
Enrollment: a project's core maintainers submit a pull request to the anthropics/oss-scanner GitHub repo using its standard template

slides.title: Fuzzing vs. a Model That Reads the Code
slides.body: OSS Scanner borrows OSS-Fuzz's eligibility bar (projects with "critical impact on infrastructure and user security") but finds bugs a different way.

rows: Logic bugs, chained flaws, protocol issues

slides.title: Worked Example: wolfSSL's Early Results
slides.body: wolfSSL, a widely embedded TLS library, was one of the projects validating the service before launch.
bullets: 72 of wolfSSL's 74 OSS Scanner reports turned out to be valid — Anthropic describes it as "all but two"
Five of those valid reports were serious enough to become CVEs

Separately, in a blind check across 48 projects, expert penetration testers reviewed 97 critical/high-severity findings: 85 (88%) cleared the bar for coordinated disclosure, 11 more were real but duplicates of known issues, and only 1 was a false positive
On the CyberGym benchmark, LLM vulnerability-finding rates went from under 20% to over 85% in about a year — the capability jump that made this service viable now rather than earlier

slides.title: The Catch: Nobody Checks the Report Before You Get It
slides.body: OSS Scanner's reports are fully model-generated with no human triage before delivery, so maintainers are the first line of review.
bullets: That 1-in-97 false-positive rate in validation is a best case — live traffic across more projects may differ
Projects without spare triage bandwidth can instead use Anthropic's separate, human-verified coordinated disclosure process
This is distinct from Claude Security, Anthropic's paid enterprise scanning and patching product — OSS Scanner is the free, community-facing sibling
Enrollment is still case-by-case, not automatic — a low-traffic hobby project is unlikely to qualify

slides.title: What Shipped, in Numbers
slides.body: Over the six months before launch, Anthropic's models had already produced tens of thousands of candidates — most were filtered before anything reached a maintainer.
bullets: 29,000+ candidate vulnerabilities generated; about 6,000 manually reviewed and triaged internally
Nearly 5,000 reports sent directly to maintainers, including some unvalidated ones at their request
Eligibility mirrors OSS-Fuzz: projects need outsized infrastructure/security impact, decided case by case

The real shift isn't the tool — it's that LLM bug-finding crossed a capability threshold (CyberGym: <20% → >85% in a year) that makes scanning every eligible OSS project with a frontier model plausible for the first time

questions.prompt: What does an OSS Scanner report include beyond a description of the bug?
options: Only a CVE number
A self-contained reproducer, a bisection to the introducing commit where possible, and a candidate patch when available
A fuzzing harness the maintainer must run themselves
A bill for the scan
questions.explanation: OSS Scanner aims to hand maintainers something actionable: code that reproduces the bug, where it was likely introduced, and a draft fix — not just a one-line alert.

questions.prompt: In the validation test across 48 projects, what fraction of the 97 critical/high findings turned out to be real?
options: About 50%
About 88% met the disclosure bar, and nearly all the rest were real but already-known duplicates
Exactly 0% — all were false positives
100%, with zero duplicates or errors
questions.explanation: 85 of 97 (88%) cleared Anthropic's coordinated-disclosure bar; 11 more were genuine but duplicated known issues, and only 1 was a false positive — a strong signal quality for a fully model-generated, unreviewed report.

questions.prompt: Why does Anthropic frame OSS Scanner as being enabled specifically now rather than a year or two earlier?
options: Open-source licenses changed to permit it
LLM vulnerability-finding performance on the CyberGym benchmark rose from under 20% to over 85% in about a year
OSS-Fuzz was discontinued
GitHub introduced a new API for it
questions.explanation: The service leans on a recent capability jump — CyberGym scores roughly quadrupling in a year — which is what made scanning at this scale and reliability newly practical.

posts.title: RLHF: Teaching a Language Model What People Actually Want
posts.subtitle: The three-model pipeline behind ChatGPT-style alignment — and why DPO and GRPO exist to escape its cost.
posts.summary: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) turns a raw next-token predictor into a model that follows instructions, by training a reward model on human preference comparisons and then optimizing the policy against it with a KL penalty that keeps it from drifting too far. It's powerful but expensive — juggling up to four models at once — which is exactly the cost that later methods like DPO and GRPO were built to cut.

slides.title: Pretraining Teaches a Model to Predict Text, Not to Help You
slides.body: A model trained only to predict the next token on internet text has no notion of 'be helpful,' 'be honest,' or 'refuse this.' RLHF is the step that bolts those preferences on.
bullets: Same base model, wildly different behavior after RLHF — it's a post-training step, not a different architecture

slides.title: You Can't Write a Loss Function for 'Helpful'
slides.body: There's no ground-truth label for the best response to an open-ended prompt — but humans can reliably compare two candidate answers and say which is better.
bullets: Comparisons are cheap and consistent for labelers; absolute quality scores are not
That asymmetry — easy to rank, hard to score — is the whole reason RLHF trains a reward model instead of hand-writing one

slides.title: The Three-Stage Pipeline
slides.body: RLHF, as popularized by OpenAI's InstructGPT, runs in three stages on top of a pretrained base model.
bullets: 1) Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): fine-tune on a smaller set of human-written demonstration responses
2) Reward model (RM): show labelers pairs of model outputs for the same prompt, collect which one they prefer, and train a separate model to predict that preference as a scalar score
3) RL fine-tuning (PPO): optimize the SFT model's weights to maximize the reward model's score on its own generated outputs

slides.title: The Leash: a KL Penalty Against the Reference Model
slides.body: Pure reward-maximization will find degenerate outputs that score well on the reward model without actually being better — so the real objective subtracts a penalty for straying from the SFT policy.
bullets: Objective per sample: reward_RM(prompt, output) − β · KL(policy_output ‖ SFT_reference_output)
β controls the leash: too loose and the model reward-hacks; too tight and it barely moves from the SFT model
Running PPO this way means four models live in memory at once: the policy, the frozen SFT reference, the reward model, and a value/critic network that estimates expected future reward

slides.title: Worked Example: Small but Aligned Beats Big but Raw
slides.body: InstructGPT's headline result: a 1.3B-parameter model fine-tuned with RLHF was preferred by human labelers over the raw 175B-parameter GPT-3 base model's outputs — despite having roughly 100x fewer parameters.
bullets: The gap wasn't capability — the 175B base model could write fine prose — it was instruction-following and judgment about what the user actually asked for
This is the result that made 'RLHF a small model' look more valuable than 'scale a raw model,' for product-facing use

slides.title: Where RLHF Breaks
slides.body: RLHF's own mechanics create failure modes that show up directly in deployed models.
bullets: Reward hacking: the policy learns quirks the reward model over-rewards — hedging, sycophancy, excessive length — without getting genuinely more helpful
Mode collapse: optimizing against one reward signal pushes outputs toward safe, bland, repetitive phrasing
Alignment tax: RLHF'd models can regress on some benchmarks (e.g. certain closed-book QA tasks) relative to the base model
Cost and instability: training and serving four models simultaneously (policy, reference, reward model, critic) is memory-heavy and sensitive to hyperparameters

slides.title: Why DPO and GRPO Exist
slides.body: Both later methods target the same expensive piece of RLHF: the extra models it has to keep around during training.

rows: Maximize RM score minus a KL penalty to the reference policy
Preference pairs feed a direct classification-style loss — no RL loop at all
Replace the critic with a group-relative baseline over sampled outputs

slides.title: The Core Idea to Keep
bullets: RLHF's job: convert 'humans can rank two answers' into a training signal, via a learned reward model
The KL penalty is what keeps reward-maximization from degenerating into reward-hacking
It's expensive specifically because of how many models PPO needs in memory at once — not because preference learning itself is expensive
DPO and GRPO aren't rejections of RLHF's goal, they're cheaper paths to the same goal, which is why RLHF is still the method taught first

questions.prompt: What does the reward model in RLHF learn to predict?
options: The probability of the next token
A scalar score reflecting which of two candidate responses humans preferred
The exact ground-truth answer to the prompt
The perplexity of the base model
questions.explanation: Humans can't reliably give an absolute quality score, but they can reliably compare two outputs — so the reward model is trained on pairwise preference comparisons and learns to output a score consistent with those rankings.

questions.prompt: Why does RLHF subtract a KL-divergence penalty from the reward score during PPO?
options: To make training run faster
To stop the policy from drifting too far from the reference model and exploiting quirks in the reward model
To eliminate the need for a reward model entirely
To shrink the model's parameter count
questions.explanation: Without the penalty, pure reward-maximization can find degenerate outputs that score high on the reward model without being genuinely better — the KL term keeps the policy anchored near the SFT model.

questions.prompt: What specific cost do DPO and GRPO each cut from the original RLHF pipeline?
options: DPO removes the reward model and the RL loop; GRPO removes the separate critic/value model
Both remove the need for any human preference data
Both replace PPO with supervised fine-tuning only
Both require training on vision data instead of text
questions.explanation: DPO turns preference pairs directly into a classification-style loss, skipping the reward model and PPO loop entirely; GRPO keeps a reward signal but drops the critic, estimating a baseline from a group of sampled outputs instead.

posts.title: Contextual Retrieval: Fixing RAG's Missing-Context Problem
posts.subtitle: The trick that cut retrieval failures by 67% without touching the embedding model.
posts.summary: Splitting documents into chunks for RAG strips away the context that made each chunk meaningful, so embedding and keyword search both miss relevant passages. Contextual Retrieval fixes this by prepending a short, LLM-written context to every chunk before indexing — cutting retrieval failure rates by up to 67% when combined with reranking.

slides.title: Why Does RAG Keep Missing the Right Chunk?
slides.body: A chunk that reads "The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter" never says which company or which quarter — so a query asking exactly that can't find it.
bullets: Splitting documents into small chunks is what makes RAG retrieval fast — and it's also what breaks it
Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval technique fixes this at the chunk level, not the embedding model level

slides.title: Chunking Throws Away the Context That Makes a Chunk Findable
slides.body: Standard RAG splits a document into independent chunks and embeds each one alone, with no memory of the document it came from.
bullets: A query for "ACME Corp revenue growth in Q2 2023" can fail against a chunk that never mentions ACME, Q2, or 2023 by name
This hurts both retrieval paths at once: dense embedding similarity and sparse keyword/BM25 search
Across Anthropic's own evaluation sets (codebases, fiction, ArXiv papers), the baseline failure rate — relevant chunks missing from the top 20 results — averaged 5.7%

slides.title: The Fix: Give Every Chunk Its Context Back Before Indexing
slides.body: An LLM reads the whole document plus one chunk, and writes a short (50-100 token) blurb situating that chunk — then that blurb is prepended to the chunk before it's indexed.
bullets: Contextual Embeddings: the context + chunk text is what actually gets embedded, so semantic search now 'sees' the company name, date, and section it belongs to
Contextual BM25: the same contextualized text also builds the keyword index, so exact-match search benefits too
Anthropic's reference implementation used Claude 3 Haiku to generate the per-chunk context at low cost
Both signals (embeddings + BM25) still feed a combined retrieval step — this augments existing RAG, it doesn't replace it

slides.title: Making the Cost Tractable: Prompt Caching
slides.body: Generating context for every chunk naively means re-sending the entire source document to the LLM once per chunk — expensive at scale.
bullets: Fix: load the full document into the prompt cache once, then reuse that cached context for every chunk's context-generation call
Anthropic's estimate: about $1.02 per million document tokens processed, for an 8k-token document split into ~800-token chunks
Caching cut latency by more than 2x and cost by up to 90% versus re-sending the document per chunk
This is a one-time preprocessing cost per document, but it recurs every time the corpus is updated

slides.title: Worked Example: The Financial-Filing Chunk
slides.body: A 10-K filing gets split into chunks. One chunk, standing alone, says only: "The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter."
bullets: Without context: a query for "ACME Corp Q2 2023 revenue growth" scores this chunk low on both embedding similarity and keyword overlap — it gets buried outside the top 20
With Contextual Retrieval: the prepended context reads something like "This chunk is from ACME Corp's Q2 2023 SEC filing; the previous quarter was Q1 2023 with revenue of $314M"
Now the chunk embeds near the query and matches on 'ACME Corp', 'Q2 2023', and 'revenue' in BM25 — it surfaces in the top results instead of being missed entirely

slides.title: How Much Each Layer Actually Helps
slides.body: Measured as failure rate: the share of relevant chunks NOT retrieved in the top 20, averaged across domains using Gemini embeddings.

slides.title: When It's Worth It — and When It Isn't
slides.body: Contextual Retrieval is a preprocessing technique, not a free lunch — weigh its cost against what you actually need.
bullets: Skip RAG entirely if your corpus is under ~200K tokens: just put the whole thing in the prompt with caching — simpler and often cheaper
Reranking adds real runtime latency and per-query cost; it buys the biggest single jump (49% → 67%) but tune how many candidates you rerank
The context-generation cost scales with corpus size and recurs on every update — budget for ongoing preprocessing, not just a one-time job
Generic document summaries prepended to chunks gave little benefit in Anthropic's tests — the gain comes from chunk-specific context, not boilerplate

questions.prompt: What specific problem does Contextual Retrieval solve in standard RAG pipelines?
options: Embedding models are too slow for production use
Chunks lose the surrounding context that would make them matchable to a query
Vector databases run out of memory with large corpora
LLMs can't generate answers from retrieved text
questions.explanation: Splitting a document into independent chunks strips out references like company names or dates that lived elsewhere in the document, so a chunk can fail to match a query that's actually about it — on both embedding and keyword search.

questions.prompt: In Anthropic's benchmark, which combination produced the largest reduction in retrieval failure rate?
options: Contextual Embeddings alone
Contextual BM25 alone
Contextual Embeddings + Contextual BM25 + reranking
Switching to a larger embedding model
questions.explanation: Stacking all three — contextual embeddings, contextual BM25, and a final reranking pass — took the failure rate from a 5.7% baseline down to 1.9%, a 67% reduction, the biggest gain coming from adding the reranker on top of the contextual signals.

questions.prompt: What makes generating per-chunk context affordable at scale, according to Anthropic's implementation?
options: Using a smaller, less accurate embedding model
Skipping context generation for most chunks
Prompt caching the full source document once, then reusing it across each chunk's context-generation call
Generating context only after retrieval, not before indexing
questions.explanation: Without caching, generating context for every chunk means resending the whole document per chunk. Caching the document once and reusing it cut both latency (>2x) and cost (up to 90%) for the preprocessing step.
