posts.title: Anthropic Gives Outside Auditors a Badge, Not Just an NDA
posts.subtitle: Six METR staffers now get Anthropic hardware, office space, and the right to publish what they find
posts.summary: Anthropic formalized a three-tier system for independent safety evaluators and put METR at the top tier: six METR staff now get employee-like access to Anthropic's systems, with publication rights Anthropic can't veto. It's a concrete template for third-party AI safety oversight, not just a promise.

slides.title: Anthropic Just Gave Outsiders a Badge to Audit Itself
slides.body: On October 15, 2026, Anthropic announced it had given six employees of METR, an independent AI safety nonprofit, insider-level access to audit its risk practices — with the right to publish what they find.
bullets: 6 METR staff get Anthropic hardware, office space, and internal tool access
This is 'tier 3' — the deepest of three new evaluator access levels
Anthropic cannot veto what METR ultimately publishes

slides.title: Why 'Trust Us, We Tested It' Doesn't Scale
slides.body: Frontier labs grade their own models' safety internally, then publish a summary. An evaluator with no equity, revenue, or operational tie to the lab is the whole point of independent review.
bullets: Anthropic signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, pledging to work with independent external evaluators
Self-assessment has no built-in mechanism to catch a lab's own blind spots
Anthropic's own criteria for a credible evaluator: expertise, independence, sufficient access, and freedom to publish

slides.title: Three Tiers, Each Trading Away More Veto Power
slides.body: Anthropic formalized evaluator access into three tiers. As access deepens, Anthropic's control over what gets said publicly shrinks.
bullets: Tier 1: narrowly scoped investigations — Anthropic approves publication
Tier 2: broader information access — publication doesn't need Anthropic's sign-off
Tier 3 (METR): employee-like access — hardware, office space, internal systems — comparable to Anthropic's own risk-assessment staff

slides.title: What Changes as You Move Up a Tier
slides.body: The real shift isn't how much an evaluator sees — it's who gets the final word on publishing it.

rows: Employee-like: badges, hardware, office space, internal tools
Publishes without approval; Anthropic can only request narrow redactions

slides.title: Anthropic Keeps Exactly Three Redaction Levers
slides.body: Even at tier 3, Anthropic can require redactions — but only in three narrow categories, and METR can publicly say if it thinks a redaction was unjustified.
bullets: Customer data
Attorney-client privileged material
Model architecture details

slides.title: Three Partnerships Already in Motion
slides.body: This isn't just METR — Anthropic named several other evaluation relationships at different stages.
bullets: SecureBio is independently reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of Anthropic's August 2026 Risk Report
Accenture and Faculty are working with Anthropic toward a partnership spanning model evaluation, red-teaming, alignment assessment, and safeguard testing
Early-stage talks are underway with other organizations, including Hugging Face

slides.title: What This Announcement Doesn't Fix
slides.body: A badge and a publication right are real commitments, but they have real limits.
bullets: It's voluntary — nothing legally compels Anthropic, or any other lab, to keep tier 3 access open
Six people is a small team to audit a frontier lab's entire risk surface
Anthropic still defines the redactable categories — 'model architecture information' is a broad label to carve out
No other major lab has matched this level of access yet, despite pledging the same Accord commitment

slides.title: The Real Test Is What METR Publishes Next
bullets: This is a structural commitment, not a result — judge it by METR's first public report, not this announcement
The three-tier model gives a concrete template other labs can copy, or be measured against
Any future redaction dispute will be the clearest signal of how real the independence actually is
Pair this with Anthropic's other 2026 safety moves (Cyber Mission, Risk Report) to see a pattern of externalizing oversight, not just claiming it

questions.prompt: What is METR, in the context of this announcement?
options: A U.S. government regulator
An independent nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models, with no equity or financial ties to Anthropic
A research team inside Anthropic
A benchmark dataset
questions.explanation: METR is independent of Anthropic by design — no equity, revenue, or operational dependence. That independence is exactly why Anthropic gave it the deepest access tier instead of treating it like a paid vendor.

options: Block publication entirely
Request redaction only in three narrow categories: customer data, privileged material, and model architecture details
Rewrite METR's conclusions before release
Decide in advance which incidents METR is allowed to see

questions.prompt: Why does an evaluator's lack of financial dependence on the lab it reviews matter?
options: It's a tax requirement
It has no real effect on credibility
It's what separates an independent evaluation from a paid endorsement
It only affects how many staff the evaluator can hire

posts.title: Function Calling: How an LLM Presses Real Buttons
posts.subtitle: Turning a probability distribution over tokens into a precise, typed API call
posts.summary: An LLM can't query a database or hit an API directly — it can only emit text. Function calling is the contract that turns that text into a structured, schema-validated request your application actually executes, and it's the mechanism underneath almost every AI agent.

slides.title: The Model Doesn't Run Code. It Asks You To.
slides.body: An LLM can't query your database or hit an API directly — it can only emit text. Function calling is the contract that turns that text into a structured request your code safely executes.
bullets: The model picks a tool and fills in arguments as JSON, not prose
Your application — never the model — actually runs the function
This loop is the foundation under almost every 'AI agent'

slides.title: Free-Text Tool Use Breaks in Production
slides.body: Early tool-use hacks asked the model to describe what it wanted in plain English and then regex-parsed the reply. That's brittle: one extra sentence or a reworded field breaks the parser.
bullets: A model might write 'the weather in Tokyo' instead of {"location": "Tokyo"}
Free text has no fixed shape — parsing it is a losing battle against model variance
Without a strict schema, wrong argument types (a string where an int belongs) slip through silently

slides.title: Give the Model a Typed Menu, Not a Blank Page
slides.body: You pass the model a list of tool definitions — name, description, and a JSON Schema for its parameters. The model returns a structured call that validates against that schema instead of free prose.
bullets: Each tool gets a name, a plain-English description, and a params schema (types, required fields, enums)
The description is often the model's only signal for picking the right tool — vague descriptions cause wrong picks
Some APIs support a 'strict' mode that guarantees the output matches the schema exactly before it's returned

slides.title: The Loop: Call, Execute, Feed Back, Repeat
slides.body: Function calling isn't one request — it's a round trip, and agents chain several of them.
bullets: 1. Model reads the prompt plus the tool list, replies with a tool_use block naming a tool and its arguments
2. Your code validates the arguments against the schema and executes the real function
3. The function's result is sent back as a tool_result in a new message
4. The model reads that result and either calls another tool or writes the final answer

slides.title: Three Ways to Get a Model to 'Use a Tool'

rows: High — validated against a schema before execution
Native — results feed back in as context
Medium — still text-parsed, but a fixed template

slides.title: Worked Example: "Convert Tokyo's Weather to Fahrenheit"
slides.body: A single user request can require two tool calls before the model ever writes a final answer.
bullets: User: "What's the weather in Tokyo, in Fahrenheit?"
Call 1 — model emits get_weather({"location": "Tokyo"}) → app returns {"tempC": 22}
Call 2 — model emits convert_temp({"value": 22, "from": "C", "to": "F"}) → app returns 71.6
Model composes: "It's about 71.6°F in Tokyo right now" — it never computed the conversion itself

slides.title: When Function Calling Is the Wrong Tool
bullets: Tool-selection accuracy degrades as the tool list grows — past a few dozen tools, retrieving only the relevant ones first beats dumping all of them in context
Every round trip costs latency — a 3-tool chain means 3+ model calls before an answer
Models can hallucinate calls: inventing a plausible-looking tool name or argument that was never defined
Never let a model-issued call perform an irreversible action (delete, send, pay) without a human-approval or dry-run step first

slides.title: Function Calling Is the Hinge Between LLMs and Agents
bullets: The model never executes anything — it only proposes a structured call your code validates and runs
A clear schema and description are the real UX surface; vague tool descriptions cause silent misuse
Chaining calls with results fed back as context is what turns a single completion into an 'agent loop'
Guard irreversible actions behind human confirmation — the model's confidence isn't a safety mechanism

questions.prompt: In function calling, what does the LLM actually do when it 'calls' a tool?
options: It executes the function's code directly inside the model
It emits a structured request (name + arguments) that your application must validate and run
It downloads the function from an API and runs it in a sandbox
It writes a plain-English paragraph describing the result
questions.explanation: The model never runs code — it only emits a structured call. Your application validates the arguments and actually executes the function, which is exactly the safety boundary that makes tool use controllable.

questions.prompt: Why does adding dozens of tools to a single prompt tend to hurt accuracy?
options: JSON schemas can't technically support more than 10 tools
The model has to pick the right tool from a longer, more confusable list, so selection accuracy drops
More tools always increase latency without bound
Tool descriptions become invalid after 10 tools
questions.explanation: Tool selection is a classification problem over the tool list — the longer and more similar the options, the more often the model picks the wrong one. That's why large toolsets often retrieve a narrowed shortlist before the model ever sees it.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't a model-issued tool call be allowed to directly delete production data?
options: Because function calling can't return error codes
Because the model's output is a sampled guess, not a verified intent, so an irreversible action needs a human or sandboxed check first
Because JSON Schema doesn't support delete operations
Because tool calls are always executed twice automatically
questions.explanation: A tool call is still a sampled output — confidently wrong calls happen. For irreversible actions, the model's output should trigger a confirmation step or a dry run, not an immediate side effect.

posts.title: 66,935 Substations, One Model, 333 Milliseconds
posts.subtitle: Microsoft Research's pipeline forecasts geomagnetic storm damage to the US grid 30-60 minutes ahead.
posts.summary: A Microsoft Research intern project built a three-stage, physics-informed ML pipeline that forecasts geomagnetically induced current risk across all 66,935 substations in the continental US grid, detecting 76.5% of major space-weather events with 30-60 minutes of lead time — while running inference on the whole grid in about 333 milliseconds.

slides.title: A Solar Storm Doesn't Wait for a Human to Notice
slides.body: Solar wind disturbances induce currents in long transmission lines that can damage transformers — and until now, grid-wide, location-specific warnings haven't existed.
bullets: Built during a Microsoft Research summer internship, mentored by the Ecology & Environment research group
Covers the entire continental US grid: 66,935 substations, built only from public data
A physics-informed pipeline, not a black box — geomagnetic forecasting feeds a per-substation risk model

slides.title: Grid Operators Get Little Warning, and None of It Is Local
slides.body: Geomagnetically induced currents (GIC) come from the same solar storms that cause auroras — but on a transmission line, they can overheat and damage transformers.
bullets: The real question isn't just 'is a storm coming' — it's 'when and where will it hit hardest,' with enough lead time to act
Existing space-weather forecasts are regional or global, not substation-specific
No widely deployed operational benchmark exists for turning a geomagnetic forecast into a per-substation damage-risk number

slides.title: Three Stages: Forecast, Localize, Aggregate
slides.body: The pipeline chains a geomagnetic forecaster into a location-aware risk model, then rolls results up into a continental map.
bullets: Stage 1: solar-wind measurements from the L1 Lagrange point forecast the AE and Dst geomagnetic indices
Stage 2: a gradient-boosting model combines those forecasts with each substation's geology and location to estimate dB/dt, the rate-of-change metric tied to GIC risk
Stage 3: per-substation estimates are aggregated into a continental risk assessment

Data sources are all public: NASA OMNI, Kyoto World Data Center, INTERMAGNET/USGS magnetometers, and GridSFM grid data; a system of 50 AI agents helped explore features and model configurations during development

slides.title: The Numbers, Stage by Stage
slides.body: Because no standard GIC-risk benchmark exists, the detection stage was compared against simple linear regression.

slides.title: From Solar Wind to Risk Map in Under Half a Second
slides.body: Walk one storm through the pipeline: solar-wind data lands from L1, and the system has an answer for every substation before an operator could finish reading an alert.
bullets: Forecast step estimates AE/Dst indices 30-60 minutes ahead of the storm's grid impact
Gradient-boosting step turns that forecast plus each substation's geology into a dB/dt estimate — this is the step that makes the warning local instead of regional
Aggregation rolls all 66,935 per-substation estimates into one continental map, computed in ~333 ms
Detection accuracy was highest at northern, high-latitude stations, where GIC exposure is already best understood

slides.title: Why This Isn't Running the Grid Yet
slides.body: The authors are explicit about the gap between a demo and a deployed safety system.
bullets: Detection drops for the most damaging events: 64.1% at extreme severity vs. 76.5% at major severity — the storms worth worrying about most are the hardest to catch
False-alarm rate rises as storm severity increases
The GIC stage has no deployed benchmark to compare against, only a linear-regression baseline — field performance is still unproven

The authors' own caveat: the continental risk map is a demonstration on a representative scenario, not a recorded live event, and 'further validation with utilities and operational data would be needed' before real grid use

slides.title: A Physics-Informed Pipeline, Not Yet a Deployed Safeguard
bullets: Three stages — geomagnetic forecast, per-substation dB/dt estimate, continental aggregation — turn a regional space-weather forecast into a local, actionable one
Real, quantified results: 76.5-81.2% detection on major/severe storms, ~333ms inference across the whole US grid
The weak point is exactly where it matters most — extreme events are the hardest to detect (64.1%)
Next steps the authors list: longer forecast horizons via temporal-transformer approaches, and integration with real grid operations

questions.prompt: What does the gradient-boosting stage of the pipeline actually predict?
options: The real-time price of electricity at each substation
dB/dt — the rate of magnetic-field change tied to geomagnetically induced current risk — combining geomagnetic forecasts with each substation's geology and location
The age and maintenance history of grid transformers
Raw solar-wind particle density at the L1 Lagrange point
questions.explanation: Stage 2 combines the forecasted geomagnetic indices (AE/Dst) with location-specific geology and conductivity features to estimate dB/dt per substation — the metric tied to GIC damage risk.

questions.prompt: How did detection performance change across storm severity tiers?
options: It was identical across all severities
It improved monotonically with severity, reaching 100% for extreme events
It was highest for major/severe storms (76.5-81.2%) but dropped to 64.1% for the most extreme events — the biggest storms were the hardest to catch
The model could only detect minor, low-risk storms
questions.explanation: Detection rates were 76.5% (major), 81.2% (severe), but fell to 64.1% for extreme events — a real limitation, since extreme storms are the ones most likely to cause serious damage.

questions.prompt: What caveat did the researchers themselves attach to this work?
options: None — they describe it as ready for immediate grid deployment
The continental risk map shown is a demonstration on a representative scenario, not a recorded live event, and further validation with real utility/operational data would be needed before grid use
The model only works outside the United States
It requires classified military data to run
questions.explanation: The authors explicitly flag that the pipeline is a research prototype — the map is illustrative, and real-world validation with utilities is a stated next step, not something already done.

posts.title: 0.002%: How Rarely Claude Breaks Election Rules
posts.subtitle: Inside Anthropic's privacy-preserving scan of 250,000 conversations before the US midterms.
posts.summary: Anthropic analyzed 250,000 sampled US Claude.ai conversations to measure real political usage ahead of the 2026 midterms, found outside red-teamers could slip multi-step misuse past single-prompt safeguards, and responded by adding classifiers for assembled campaigns, fake news operations, and foreign state actors.

slides.title: 250,000 Conversations, One Privacy-Preserving Scan
slides.body: Ahead of the 2026 US midterms, Anthropic published what it actually measured about political use of Claude — not just what it hopes is true.
bullets: Published October 14, 2026, building on an earlier election-safeguards update
Covers four areas: real usage, pointing users to trusted sources, bias testing, and misuse detection

slides.title: Blocking One Bad Prompt Doesn't Block a Campaign
slides.body: Outside testers found the real gap wasn't single harmful requests — it was requests split into pieces that each looked harmless alone.
bullets: The Institute for Strategic Dialogue and the McCain Institute red-teamed safeguards in the US, Israel, and Brazil
Finding, quoted directly: Claude 'could miss a malicious campaign when it was spread across many individual requests'
A model that reliably refuses one bad ask can still be assembled, step by step, into disinformation infrastructure

slides.title: Clio: Measuring Usage Without Reading Transcripts
slides.body: Anthropic used Clio, a privacy-preserving analysis method, on a random sample of US conversations from Sept 21-27, 2026.
bullets: 5.75% of sampled US conversations touched politics, public policy, or social issues
0.51% were specifically about elections or voting
0.01% asked Claude directly whom or what to vote for — most political use was informational (research, weighing arguments)
0.002% violated Anthropic's election-integrity policies outright

posts.title: DPO: Skipping the Reward Model Entirely
posts.subtitle: A policy's own log-probabilities can be its reward model — no RL loop required.
posts.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) reformulates the same KL-constrained objective behind RLHF so that the optimal policy's log-probability ratio against a reference model is itself an implicit reward. That turns a multi-stage pipeline — train a reward model, then run PPO against it — into a single supervised-style loss over preference pairs, at the cost of training entirely offline on fixed data.

slides.title: The Reward Model You Don't Need to Train
slides.body: DPO reframes RLHF's two-stage pipeline — train a reward model, then run reinforcement learning against it — into one loss function computed directly on a language model's own log-probabilities.
bullets: No reward model is trained, and no RL rollouts are sampled during training
Same inputs as RLHF — pairs of (chosen, rejected) responses — just a different, closed-form way to use them

slides.title: RLHF's Pipeline Has a Lot of Moving Parts
slides.body: Standard RLHF needs a reward model trained on preference pairs, then PPO fine-tuning against it with a critic and a KL penalty to stop the policy from drifting too far.
bullets: Four models typically sit in memory at once during PPO: the policy, a frozen reference copy, the reward model, and the critic
PPO introduces its own hyperparameters — clip ratio, GAE lambda, KL coefficient — each one a place training can go unstable
The reward model itself can be exploited (reward hacking) before the policy ever gets near real quality gains

slides.title: One Loss, Two Copies of the Same Model
slides.body: DPO starts from the same KL-constrained objective as RLHF — maximize reward while staying close to a reference policy — and solves it in closed form instead of iterating with RL.
bullets: Under a Bradley-Terry preference model, the optimal policy for that objective has a known closed form, which means the *implied* reward is proportional to log(policy / reference) for a given response

Substituting that implicit reward back into the preference loss gives DPO's actual training objective: push up log-probability of the chosen response relative to the reference, push down the rejected one, scaled by a single temperature-like constant β
Only two model copies are needed at train time: the policy being trained and a frozen reference — no reward model, no critic, no sampling loop

slides.title: One Preference Pair, Worked Through
slides.body: Say a prompt has a preferred response A and a rejected response B.
bullets: Compute how much more likely the current policy makes A and B than the frozen reference does, for each response
If the policy already favors A over B by more than the reference did, the pair contributes a small loss and a small gradient
If the policy still favors B (the rejected one), the loss is large, and the gradient pushes log-probability toward A and away from B, scaled by β
No sampling is needed to compute any of this — it's a forward pass through two models on existing text, exactly like a supervised fine-tuning step

slides.title: RLHF's Pipeline vs. DPO

rows: Implicit — the policy's own log-prob ratio against the reference
Online: sample rollouts, score, update, repeat
Offline: one pass over a fixed preference dataset
Clip ratio, GAE lambda, KL coefficient, reward scale
Single β controlling drift from the reference

slides.title: The Simplicity Has a Cost
slides.body: DPO trades RL's instability for a different set of failure modes.
bullets: Being offline cuts both ways: no new rollouts means the policy only ever adjusts on pairs someone already collected — it can't explore its own outputs to find and fix new failure modes mid-training

'Likelihood displacement': empirically, the chosen response's probability doesn't always go up — sometimes both chosen and rejected probabilities fall, just the rejected one falls faster, which still reduces the loss but doesn't guarantee better generations
No separate reward model means no reusable artifact for scoring or filtering future data — RLHF's reward model can double as a data-quality filter; DPO's doesn't exist as a standalone object
Quality is capped by the preference dataset's own consistency — there's no RL exploration to work around biased or noisy labels

slides.title: Same Goal, Fewer Parts, Different Risks
bullets: DPO reaches the same KL-constrained alignment objective as RLHF, but solves it in closed form instead of running RL
Cuts training to 2 models instead of 4, and replaces online rollouts with a single offline pass over preference pairs — much simpler infrastructure
The cost is losing on-policy exploration: it only ever refines on data already collected, and can't correct for gaps that only RL rollouts would surface
Became popular because it reuses standard supervised fine-tuning infrastructure while reaching comparable quality to PPO-based RLHF on many tasks

questions.prompt: What does DPO use in place of a separately trained reward model?
options: A fixed reward of +1 for chosen responses and -1 for rejected ones
The ratio between the policy's and a frozen reference model's log-probabilities for a given response, scaled by β
A human grader reviewing every training batch
The same critic network PPO uses, just renamed
questions.explanation: Solving the KL-constrained RL objective in closed form shows the optimal policy's implied reward is proportional to log(policy/reference) — so DPO's loss uses that ratio directly, with no separate reward model ever trained.

questions.prompt: Why is DPO described as 'offline' compared to PPO-based RLHF?
options: It can only run without an internet connection
It trains on a fixed, already-collected set of preference pairs rather than sampling new rollouts from the current policy during training
It doesn't require a GPU
It only works on text generated before 2023
questions.explanation: PPO-based RLHF samples fresh completions from the current policy throughout training (on-policy). DPO instead does a single pass over a fixed dataset of preference pairs collected in advance — no new sampling happens mid-training.

questions.prompt: What is 'likelihood displacement' in DPO training?
options: The policy's vocabulary size shrinking during training
The chosen response's probability doesn't always rise — sometimes both chosen and rejected probabilities fall, with the rejected one falling faster
The reward model being replaced mid-training
A bug that only affects models larger than 100B parameters
questions.explanation: Because the loss only depends on the *relative* gap between chosen and rejected log-probabilities, it can be reduced by pushing the rejected response down faster than lifting the chosen one up — so the chosen response's absolute probability can still decrease.

posts.title: Prompt Caching: Stop Paying to Re-Read the Same Context
posts.subtitle: Why a cache write costs more, a cache read costs almost nothing, and order matters
posts.summary: Prompt caching lets an LLM provider skip recomputing attention over tokens it has already seen, by storing the KV state for a shared prefix. It turns a 1.25x premium on the first call into a 10-40x discount on every repeat call — but only if your prompt structure actually produces repeat calls.

slides.title: Every API call reprocesses your entire prompt from scratch
slides.body: System prompts, tool schemas, long documents, few-shot examples — by default, the model runs full attention over all of it, every single call.
bullets: An agent with a 50K-token toolset pays for those 50K tokens on every turn
Prompt caching exists to stop that waste

slides.title: The waste compounds fast in agent loops
slides.body: A multi-turn agent session resends the same static context — system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved documents — on every single call, because each API request is stateless.
bullets: 20-turn session with a 50K-token static context = 1M tokens billed, 95% of it identical to the call before
The redundant tokens still cost full attention compute and full price

slides.title: How it works: hashing a shared prefix
slides.body: The provider hashes the token sequence up to a cache breakpoint. A later request with an identical prefix hits the cache: its KV state is reloaded instead of recomputed, so the model only runs full attention on the new tokens after the breakpoint.
bullets: Cache WRITE (first time a prefix is seen): costs MORE than normal input — the provider pays to compute and store the KV state
Cache READ (prefix seen again before it expires): costs a small fraction of input price — just a lookup, no recomputation
Match must be exact: one changed token before the breakpoint invalidates the whole cache for everything after it

slides.title: Real pricing multipliers (Anthropic, per 1M tokens)
slides.body: Cache writes run 1.25x base input price; cache reads run far below it — and the discount gets steeper on cheaper models.
bullets: Default cache TTL is 5 minutes; an 'extended' 1-hour TTL option exists for longer-lived sessions

slides.title: Worked example: a 20-call coding agent session
slides.body: Sonnet 5.5, $2/M input, 50K-token static context (codebase + tool schemas) resent every call:
bullets: Cached total: ~$0.22 — about 89% cheaper for identical output
The savings scale with session length: a 100-call session gets even closer to the 95% ceiling

slides.title: Where it quietly fails
slides.body: Caching only pays off if your prompt structure actually produces a stable, reusable prefix.
bullets: Put dynamic content (user message, timestamp, random IDs) first and you invalidate the cache on every call
Idle past the TTL (5 min default) and the next call is billed as a fresh write, not a read
One-off prompts that never repeat just eat the 1.25x write premium for nothing
Fix: order prompts static-to-dynamic — system prompt and tool defs first, user turn last

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: A cache hit skips recomputing attention for already-seen tokens — it reuses stored KV state
Writes cost 1.25x, reads cost 0.025x-0.1x depending on the model — the breakeven is usually just 2 calls
Structure prompts static-first, dynamic-last so the shared prefix actually matches across calls
TTL matters: a 5-minute default means idle agents lose the cache and eat the write cost again

questions.prompt: Why does a prompt-cache WRITE cost more than a normal input token?
options: It's a pricing penalty to discourage overuse of caching
The provider has to compute and store the KV state for later reuse
Writes always use a larger, more expensive model
It doesn't — writes and reads cost the same
questions.explanation: A cache write means the provider computes full attention AND persists the resulting KV state so a future call can skip that computation — that extra storage work is why it's priced at a premium (typically 1.25x).

questions.prompt: You're designing a prompt for an agent loop. Where should the static content (system prompt, tool schemas) go to maximize cache hits?
options: At the end, right before the model's response
Anywhere — order doesn't matter for caching
At the start, since caching matches on a shared prefix
Split evenly between the start and end
questions.explanation: Caching works by matching an identical token prefix. Putting static content first and the dynamic user turn last means every call shares the same cacheable prefix; the reverse order invalidates the cache every time.

questions.prompt: Your agent session sits idle for 10 minutes on the default 5-minute TTL, then makes another call. What happens to the cache?
options: It's still valid — TTL only applies to the first write
It has expired, so the next call is billed as a fresh cache write
The call fails with an error
The cache is extended automatically for active sessions
questions.explanation: The default cache entry lives for 5 minutes. Once that expires, the next matching request can't hit it — it's treated as a new cache write at the 1.25x rate, not a cheap read.

posts.title: Vela: Training LLMs on What Users Actually Do
posts.subtitle: A social platform turned 100,000 users' real behavior into the training signal
posts.summary: Vela turns real, anonymized user-behavior logs from a large social platform into 100,000 trainable tasks, then fine-tunes an LLM on them. slides.title: The Internet's #1 Paper Today Trains on Clicks, Not Captions
slides.body: Vela (arXiv 2610.14709) topped Hugging Face's Daily Papers leaderboard by proposing something simple: skip synthetic instructions and train directly on what real users did.
bullets: 19 authors, posted Oct 10, 2026
Code: github.com/AllSpark-Research/Vela

slides.title: Synthetic Instruction Data Has a Ceiling
slides.body: Most post-training data is either hand-written or LLM-generated — clean, but disconnected from how people actually phrase requests, change their minds, or chain tasks together.
bullets: Synthetic tasks rarely capture messy, multi-step real intent
Models trained only on curated instructions plateau on personalization and long-horizon tasks
Real behavior logs exist at huge scale but are rarely turned into training data

slides.title: Turn Anonymized Behavior Into Trainable Trajectories
slides.body: Vela's pipeline starts from anonymized activity records of 100,000 users on a large social platform and mines them into structured tasks.
bullets: 100,000 users → 100,000 tasks spanning 91 distinct task templates
Difficulty-based filtering + trajectory-acceptance criteria trim this to ~75,000 high-quality training trajectories
Each trajectory pairs a real behavioral context with the action a user actually took

slides.title: What a Task Template Looks Like
slides.body: One of the 91 templates might take a user's recent activity (posts viewed, searches, replies) and ask the model to predict or summarize their next likely action — then score the model against what the user really did next.
bullets: Template diversity matters: 91 templates stop the model from overfitting to one narrow skill
Trajectories are filtered for difficulty so the model isn't trained on trivially easy predictions

slides.title: The Numbers: Fine-Tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
slides.body: The paper evaluates on VelaBench (982 held-out tasks from the same 91 templates) plus general out-of-distribution suites.

slides.title: Why This Matters Beyond One Benchmark
bullets: Real behavior logs are an underused supervision source — the gain came from data, not a new architecture
Gains transferred to general OOD tasks, not just the in-domain benchmark, suggesting the signal teaches a real skill (modeling user intent)
RL on top of behavior fine-tuning stacked further gains, hinting the two are complementary, not redundant
Any system using this approach inherits a hard privacy/anonymization obligation — the data source is the thing that makes it powerful and sensitive

posts.title: Mamba: The Architecture That Trades Attention for a Fixed-Size Memory
posts.subtitle: Selective state space models process any sequence length in linear time
posts.summary: Mamba replaces self-attention with a selective state space model (SSM): a recurrence whose step size and projections are themselves functions of the input. That selection mechanism, paired with a hardware-aware parallel scan, gives transformer-competitive quality with linear-time compute and a fixed-size state — at the cost of weaker exact long-range recall, which is why hybrid Mamba+attention architectures now exist.

slides.title: What If the Model Never Re-Read the Whole Conversation?
slides.body: Every transformer layer re-attends to every previous token at every step. Mamba asks: what if the model just kept a running summary instead?

slides.title: Attention's Bill Comes Due at Long Context
slides.body: Self-attention computes a score between every pair of tokens, so compute grows quadratically with sequence length — and the KV cache that stores past keys/values grows linearly in memory, forever.
bullets: Doubling context length roughly quadruples attention compute
KV cache memory grows with every token generated, even for tokens that stop mattering
This is the core bottleneck behind most long-context inference costs

slides.title: A Recurrence That Learns What to Keep
slides.body: Classic state space models (SSMs) compress a sequence into a fixed-size hidden state via a linear recurrence — cheap, but the recurrence's parameters are fixed, so it can't choose what's important.
bullets: Mamba makes the recurrence's step size and its input/output projections (Δ, B, C) functions of the current input — a 'selection mechanism'
This lets the model dynamically decide what to fold into the running state and what to let decay
A hardware-aware parallel scan makes this recurrence train efficiently on GPUs despite being sequential in principle

slides.title: Worked Example: A 100,000-Token Document
slides.body: A transformer processing a 100K-token document must store and attend over a KV cache that grows with every token — memory and compute both scale with length.
bullets: Mamba instead compresses everything seen so far into one fixed-size state vector, updated token by token
Generating token 100,000 costs roughly the same as generating token 100 — state size never changes
The tradeoff: that fixed-size state is a compressed summary, not a lossless record

slides.title: Mamba vs. Transformer Attention

rows: Strong — attends directly to any past token

slides.title: When NOT to Reach for Pure Mamba
bullets: Tasks needing exact retrieval of a specific fact from far back (needle-in-a-haystack, precise copying) favor attention's direct lookups
A fixed-size state is a bottleneck: it must compress unboundedly long history into constant space

This is exactly why hybrid architectures (e.g., Jamba, Zamba) interleave a few attention layers among many SSM layers — cheap linear-time layers for bulk processing, occasional attention layers for precise recall

slides.title: The Core Trade
bullets: Mamba swaps attention's 'remember everything exactly' for a recurrence that 'remembers what it learned to prioritize'
Linear-time compute and constant-memory state make it attractive for long sequences and cheap inference
The precise-recall weakness is real, not hypothetical — it's why production systems increasingly hybridize SSM layers with a handful of attention layers rather than going pure-SSM
Think of it as a complementary tool to attention, not a strict replacement

questions.prompt: What makes Mamba's state space model 'selective'?
options: It randomly drops tokens during training
Its recurrence parameters (step size, input/output projections) are functions of the current input, letting it choose what to keep
It selects only a subset of model layers to run at inference time
It uses a vote among multiple smaller models
questions.explanation: The 'selection mechanism' is what separates Mamba from classic, fixed-parameter SSMs: Δ, B, and C become input-dependent, so the model learns what to fold into its running state versus let decay.

questions.prompt: Why does Mamba cost roughly the same to generate token 100,000 as token 100, while a transformer doesn't?
options: Mamba uses a smaller vocabulary
Mamba compresses history into a fixed-size state that doesn't grow, while a transformer's KV cache keeps growing
Mamba skips every other token
Transformers always use more parameters than Mamba models
questions.explanation: Mamba's state size is fixed regardless of how many tokens came before, so per-token cost stays flat. A transformer's KV cache grows with every generated token, so later tokens cost more to attend over.

questions.prompt: Why do hybrid architectures mix Mamba (SSM) layers with a few attention layers instead of using pure Mamba?
options: Pure Mamba models are too slow to train
Attention layers are cheaper than SSM layers
Mamba's fixed-size state compresses history lossily, so occasional attention layers recover the exact long-range recall Mamba struggles with
Mixing architectures is required by most model licenses
questions.explanation: Mamba trades exact recall for linear-time efficiency. Hybrids keep most layers cheap (SSM) but add a few attention layers specifically to restore precise long-range lookups where it matters.

posts.title: Gemini 4 Argon Lands on Google Cloud
posts.subtitle: Google's new frontier model ties for first on a security benchmark and cut prompt-injection attacks to 0.7%.
posts.summary: Google made Gemini 4 Argon — its new frontier model, API id gemini-4-argon — available to everyone on Google Cloud on October 13, 2026. It leads the Vals Index and Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark, ties for first on CWE-Bench v1 at 68%, and cuts indirect prompt-injection attack success to 0.7%. A separate, un-guardrailed build ships only to vetted defenders through the Fairwind Program.

slides.title: Google Ships Its New Frontier Model: Gemini 4 Argon
slides.body: On October 13, 2026, Google Cloud VP Michael Gerstenhaber announced general availability of Gemini 4 Argon (model id gemini-4-argon) — what Google calls 'our new frontier model.'
bullets: Follows the prior week's launch of the Gemini agent, a 'universal agent for work'
Live now in Gemini for Business (web/desktop/mobile), the Gemini API, AI Studio, and Antigravity
Pitched as built 'to work with both depth and precision' across long, multi-step tasks

slides.title: Long Agentic Tasks Punish Small Mistakes
slides.body: A model that can keep working for hours is only useful if it doesn't quietly drift — fabricating a citation, missing a system boundary, or taking an irreversible action without asking.
bullets: Finance, legal research, and large codebase work all require long sessions where one wrong step compounds
Google frames the core tension as depth (keep going until the job is done) vs. precision (don't make things up along the way)
The announcement explicitly calls out training Argon to 'report negative findings honestly' and 'pause for confirmation before taking irreversible steps'

slides.title: Trained to Read Mixed Documents and Keep Going
slides.body: Argon is positioned around three domains in the launch post: finance, legal research, and coding — each needing sustained, grounded work rather than one-shot answers.
bullets: Reads documents mixing text, tables, charts, and images, producing grounded, structured output
'On long tasks, it keeps going until the job is done' — Google's framing for sustained agentic sessions
Finance use cases named: ledger reconciliations, spreadsheet formulas, variance analysis
Legal use cases named: verified citations and precedent research — Harvey's Head of Applied Research called it a 'substantial improvement over Gemini 3.1 Pro'

slides.title: The Benchmark Numbers Google Published
slides.body: Four results anchor the launch post — each tied to a named benchmark, not a vague claim.

slides.title: Months of Refactoring Done in Weeks
slides.body: The clearest concrete example in the post is a sustained engineering task, not a benchmark score.
bullets: Used internally to finish an architectural refactor across 'hundreds of files' in Chromium's 40-million-line codebase
Google describes it as completing 'months of work in weeks' — a direct claim about the long-task framing, not a one-off demo
On Google's internal Antigravity tool, agentic code submissions rose 35%+ while rollbacks fell by nearly a third
Security firm HubX reported identifying 100% of top-priority vulnerabilities in a test with 0% fabricated findings across verified claims

slides.title: Two Builds: Guardrailed, and Guardrails-Off for Vetted Defenders
slides.body: Argon ships with built-in cyber mitigations that block offensive tasks like pentesting and exploitation by default.
bullets: Defensive security work routes through CodeMender or a customer's own security harness instead
A separate build with cyber guardrails removed is available only through the Fairwind Program — limited to government, critical-infrastructure, and cybersecurity partners
Mirrors the tiered-access pattern Anthropic uses for its own models: broad access with safety limits, narrow access with fewer limits for vetted defenders

Every customer quote (GitLab, Harvey, ServiceNow, Figma, HubX) comes from Google's own post, not an independent benchmark run
Pricing is introductory through November 30, 2026: $2/$10 per 1M input/output tokens, rising to $4/$20 after — budget accordingly if you're testing now

bullets: Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon) is Google's new frontier model, GA on Google Cloud since October 13, 2026
Leads Vals Index and Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark, ties for first on CWE-Bench v1, cuts prompt-injection success to 0.7%

posts.title: GRPO: Reinforcement Learning Without a Critic
posts.subtitle: Why reasoning models skip the value network and let a group of samples grade itself.
posts.summary: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) trains an LLM with reinforcement learning by sampling a group of outputs per prompt and scoring each one against the group's own average, instead of training a separate critic network to estimate value. That cuts memory and compute roughly in half and pairs naturally with verifiable, outcome-only rewards like 'is this proof correct' — the setup behind most modern reasoning-model training.

slides.title: One Model, No Second Model to Grade It
slides.body: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is the reinforcement-learning algorithm introduced in DeepSeekMath and later scaled up for DeepSeek-R1's reasoning training.
bullets: Core move: sample a group of completions per prompt, score each, and use the group's own statistics as the baseline
No separate value network is trained — that's the 'without a critic' part
Became the template for training reasoning models on tasks with a checkable right answer

slides.title: PPO's Critic Costs as Much as the Model It's Grading
slides.body: Standard RLHF uses PPO, which needs a learned value function (the critic) to estimate how good a partial response is, so it can compute an advantage at every token.
bullets: The critic is typically a full second network close to the policy's size — roughly doubling memory and compute during training
For math and code, rewards are sparse and binary (correct/incorrect at the end), which makes a token-level critic noisy and hard to train well
A badly trained critic doesn't just waste compute — it injects biased advantage estimates that quietly steer the policy in the wrong direction

slides.title: Let the Group Be the Baseline
slides.body: GRPO replaces the learned critic with simple group statistics, computed fresh for every prompt.
bullets: For each prompt, sample a group of G completions (commonly 8–64) from the current policy
Score every completion with a reward function — often a rule-based verifier (did the proof check out, did the tests pass)
Advantage for completion i = (reward_i − mean of the group's rewards) / (standard deviation of the group's rewards)

Update the policy with a clipped PPO-style ratio objective, but using this group-normalized advantage instead of a learned value estimate; a KL term against a reference model is added directly in the loss rather than subtracted from the reward

slides.title: PPO vs. GRPO, Side by Side
slides.body: The difference isn't cosmetic — it changes what hardware and reward signal you need.

rows: Added directly as a loss term

slides.title: Walking Through One Math Prompt
slides.body: Say the policy samples G = 8 candidate solutions to a math problem, and a verifier checks the final answer against the known solution.
bullets: 3 completions land on the correct answer (reward = 1), 5 don't (reward = 0)
Group mean = 3/8 = 0.375, group standard deviation ≈ 0.48
Each correct completion gets a positive advantage (≈ +1.3); each incorrect one gets a negative advantage (≈ −0.78)
The gradient step pushes the policy toward the token patterns in the correct completions and away from the incorrect ones — entirely from this one batch of 8 samples, no critic involved

slides.title: Why Reasoning Models Lean on This
slides.body: Long chains of thought make token-level credit assignment brutal: which of 2,000 reasoning tokens actually caused the right final answer?
bullets: GRPO sidesteps the question — it only needs the final, verifiable outcome, and lets the whole chain share the credit or blame
That's a good match for math, code, and other tasks with a cheap, automatic checker; it's why GRPO-style training became the common recipe behind reasoning-focused open models
The group itself substitutes for the critic's job: instead of asking 'is this better than the critic's estimate,' it asks 'is this better than what I just tried 8 times'

slides.title: Where GRPO Breaks Down
slides.body: Dropping the critic isn't free — it trades one failure mode for another.
bullets: If every completion in a group gets the same reward (all correct, or all wrong), the standard deviation is 0 and the advantage is undefined or zero — that batch teaches the model nothing and the rollouts are wasted
Needs a clean, cheap, verifiable reward; for subjective tasks (open-ended writing, nuanced helpfulness) there's no reliable checker, so GRPO has little advantage over PPO there
More rollouts per prompt (G=8–64) means more inference-time sampling cost during training, even though it removes the critic's training cost — it shifts compute, it doesn't just delete it
A model can still learn a reward-hacking shortcut (e.g., matching a verifier's answer format without real reasoning) — the group-relative setup doesn't fix a badly designed reward function

slides.title: The Trade GRPO Makes
bullets: GRPO drops PPO's learned critic and replaces it with a group of sampled completions scoring each other via mean and standard deviation
Cuts training memory roughly in half by removing the critic network, at the cost of sampling more completions per prompt
Needs a cheap, verifiable reward (correct/incorrect) to work well — it's the engine behind most reasoning-model RL training, not a general RLHF replacement
Watch for zero-variance groups (all-correct or all-wrong batches) — they silently waste compute because the advantage collapses to zero

questions.prompt: What does GRPO use instead of PPO's learned critic network to compute an advantage?
options: A second, smaller neural network trained only on failures
The group's own mean and standard deviation of rewards across sampled completions for the same prompt
A fixed advantage of 1 for every completion
Human preference labels collected in real time
questions.explanation: GRPO samples a group of completions per prompt and normalizes each one's reward against that group's mean and standard deviation — no separate value network is trained.

questions.prompt: Why does a reward function that's sparse and binary (correct/incorrect) suit GRPO particularly well?
options: Because GRPO can only process rewards between 0 and 1
Because it requires no verifier at all
Because GRPO only needs a final, checkable outcome to rank completions in a group — it doesn't need a token-level value estimate for partial progress
Because sparse rewards make the critic network train faster
questions.explanation: GRPO's group-relative comparison only needs the final outcome reward per completion; it was never training a token-level critic in the first place, so sparse, verifiable rewards (math, code) are a natural fit.

questions.prompt: What happens in GRPO if every completion sampled for a prompt gets the exact same reward?
options: The policy is updated twice as strongly
The group's standard deviation is zero, so the advantage collapses and that batch provides no learning signal
GRPO automatically falls back to a PPO critic for that batch
The prompt is permanently removed from training
questions.explanation: GRPO's advantage is a z-score: (reward − group mean) / group standard deviation. If all completions score identically, the standard deviation is 0 and there's no relative signal to learn from, wasting that batch's rollouts.

posts.title: Anthropic's Cyber Program Gets Three Tiers of Access
posts.subtitle: Legitimate pentesters now get a Claude that fights back less — but only if they can prove who they are.
posts.summary: Anthropic merged its Cyber Verification Program and Project Glasswing into a single three-tier system — Defense, Red Team, and Specialized Access — that progressively lowers Claude's safety blocks for vetted security professionals. Benchmark data shows the difference is stark: fully blocked with no program, mostly blocked at the Defense tier, and performing like an unrestricted model at the Red Team tier.

slides.title: A Model That Blocks Attacks Can't Also Simulate Them
slides.body: On October 6, 2026, Anthropic launched an expanded Cyber Verification Program (CVP), merging it with the older Project Glasswing into one tiered system for vetted security professionals.
bullets: Three tiers: Defense Access, Red Team Access, Specialized Access
Every tier runs on Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1
Replaces a binary 'blocked or not' setup with graduated trust

slides.title: Safety Classifiers Don't Know You're Authorized
slides.body: Claude's default safeguards can't distinguish a criminal probing for ransomware deployment from a SOC analyst reverse-engineering the same malware sample for a client.
bullets: Incident response, malware reverse-engineering, and authorized penetration testing all resemble attacks on the surface
A model tuned to refuse attacks by default will also refuse the defenders who need to reproduce them
Anthropic's fix isn't a blanket unlock — it's identity-gated access that scales with how much harm a mistake could cause

slides.title: Three Tiers, Each Trading More Access for More Vetting
slides.body: Access is granted per-organization (mostly), not per-request, and each tier adds capability while narrowing eligibility.
bullets: Defense Access: incident response, reverse-engineering, vuln analysis — open to companies, universities, nonprofits, and even individual researchers with a reporting track record; reviewed in days

Red Team Access: adds authorized penetration testing against systems you're cleared to test; organizations only, review takes weeks, hard blocks stay on physical-harm actions like deploying ransomware
Specialized Access: fewest blocks of all, reserved for orgs vetted directly with the US government to test safety-critical systems — flight systems, power grids, interbank transfer networks
Former Glasswing members slot straight into Specialized Access on current models, no reapproval needed

slides.title: The Benchmark Makes the Tiers Concrete
slides.body: Anthropic ran Claude Opus 5.5 through CyScenarioBench — 10 cyber challenges, 5 attempts each (50 trials) — at each access level.

slides.title: The Same Prompt, Three Different Outcomes
slides.body: Picture a contracted red-team firm asked to actually attempt a ransomware-style payload against a client's test environment, under signed authorization.
bullets: On a default Claude account: refused immediately — the request pattern-matches to an attack regardless of context
On Defense Access: likely still blocked — this tier covers analysis and reverse-engineering, not active offensive testing

On Red Team Access: proceeds, because the org is pre-vetted and the target is one they're authorized to test — except the real-time block on deploying actual ransomware payloads stays on at every tier
That last carve-out is deliberate: authorization changes what Claude will help plan, not whether it will trigger irreversible physical or infrastructure harm

slides.title: What Project Glasswing Already Found
slides.body: The expanded program isn't starting from zero — it's built on results from the narrower program it replaces.
bullets: Glasswing partners found at least 129,000 verified software vulnerabilities between April and July 2026
Anthropic's own open-source scanning turned up 5,500 more vulnerabilities through October
Over 33,000 of the combined total are rated critical or high severity
Anthropic calls these figures a lower bound — partial partner reporting means the real number could be 5x higher

slides.title: The Fine Print Before You Apply
slides.body: Loosened safety blocks come with strings attached, and they're not optional yet.
bullets: Data retention is required so Anthropic can monitor for misuse — zero-retention access only exists today via Claude Fable 5.1 or Mythos 5.1, until Enterprise Frontier Safeguards ships later this fall
Red Team Access is organizations-only; individual researchers top out at Defense Access
Available on the Claude Platform, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry now; Amazon Bedrock only for Enterprise Frontier Safeguards–eligible customers
A wrongly-applied block can be appealed through a form — this is still a classifier making judgment calls, not a true off-switch

slides.title: Access Is Now a Spectrum, Not a Switch
bullets: CVP + Glasswing merged into three tiers — Defense, Red Team, Specialized — each trading deeper vetting for fewer safety blocks
The benchmark gap is the real story: 0/50 unblocked trials at no access vs. 34/50 at Red Team Access, matching an unrestricted model
Individuals can get Defense Access; Red Team and Specialized require an organization and, for the top tier, direct government vetting
Data retention is mandatory until Enterprise Frontier Safeguards ships — zero-retention workarounds exist only on specific models for now

questions.prompt: What changed between the original CVP and this expanded version?
options: Nothing — it's a rebrand with no new capabilities
It merged CVP and Project Glasswing into three access tiers (Defense, Red Team, Specialized) instead of one flat program
It removed all safety restrictions for every Claude user
It only applies to government agencies
questions.explanation: The expansion combines two previously separate programs into a single tiered structure, so the level of access now scales with how thoroughly an organization is vetted.

questions.prompt: On the CyScenarioBench benchmark, what happened at Red Team Access that didn't happen at Defense Access?
options: Every trial was blocked
The model completed 34 of 50 trials with no blocks, matching its unrestricted completion rate
Only reverse-engineering tasks were allowed
The benchmark wasn't run at that tier
questions.explanation: At Red Team Access, none of the 50 trials were blocked and the completion rate (34/50) matched the model's behavior with no safeguards at all — a measurable jump from Defense Access, where 46 of 50 trials were blocked at some point.

questions.prompt: Why does Anthropic keep a hard block on actions like deploying ransomware even for Red Team Access organizations?
options: Because Red Team Access doesn't cover penetration testing at all
Because authorization changes what Claude will help plan or simulate, but not whether it will trigger irreversible physical or infrastructure harm
Because Red Team Access is identical to Defense Access
Because only Specialized Access organizations exist
questions.explanation: Even pre-vetted, authorized red teams can't get Claude to actually execute a destructive payload — the tier system raises what Claude will help analyze or simulate, but certain real-world-harm actions stay blocked regardless of who's asking.

posts.title: Sliding Window Attention: Capping the Cost of Looking Back
posts.subtitle: Why make every token scan the whole conversation when the last few thousand usually tell the story?
posts.summary: Sliding window attention caps each token's attention to a fixed-size local window instead of the entire sequence, turning quadratic attention cost into something closer to linear. Production models pair it with occasional full-attention layers so local efficiency doesn't come at the cost of losing distant context entirely.

slides.title: Full Attention Means Every Token Reads Everything
slides.body: In standard self-attention, token number 50,000 still computes a score against all 49,999 tokens before it. That's the mechanism that makes transformers powerful — and the reason long context is so expensive.
bullets: Compute cost per layer grows quadratically with sequence length: double the tokens, quadruple the attention work
The KV cache that holds past keys and values also grows linearly with every token generated
Sliding window attention tackles both by restricting what each token is allowed to look at

slides.title: The Mechanism: Attend to the Last W Tokens, Not All of Them
slides.body: Each token attends only to itself and a fixed number of preceding tokens — the window — and nothing further back, no matter how long the sequence gets.
bullets: Reduces per-layer attention cost from O(n²) to roughly O(n·W), where W is the window size
The KV cache per layer is capped at W entries instead of growing with the whole sequence
Mistral 7B popularized this at production scale with a window of 4,096 tokens per layer
Longformer (2020) was an earlier version of the idea, pairing a local window with a handful of 'global' tokens that attend to everything

slides.title: Layers Stack the Window, So the Effective Range Grows
slides.body: A single layer only sees W tokens back, but information can still travel further because each layer's output becomes the next layer's input.
bullets: After L stacked sliding-window layers, information from up to roughly L×W tokens back can in principle reach the current token
This mirrors how stacking small convolutional kernels in a CNN builds a larger effective receptive field
In practice the signal weakens the further back it has to travel through multiple hops, so this isn't the same as direct access to a distant token
Many architectures interleave a handful of full-attention layers among the sliding-window ones specifically to patch this gap

slides.title: Full Attention vs. Sliding Window

rows: Only within W, except via multi-layer propagation
Short-to-medium context, tasks needing exact recall of any token
Long sequences, local-dependency-heavy tasks (code, chat), cost-sensitive serving

slides.title: Where It Breaks: The Needle Far Outside the Window
slides.body: Say a 50,000-token document states a critical fact once near the start, and the model needs to recall it while generating near the end, with a 4,096-token window.
bullets: A pure sliding-window layer at the end of the sequence has no direct path to that early token — it's tens of thousands of tokens outside the window
Multi-layer propagation can carry a trace of it forward, but each hop risks losing precision, especially for an exact name, number, or date
This is precisely why production models don't rely on sliding window layers alone for long-context tasks
The fix in practice: interleave periodic full-attention layers, or combine with techniques like attention sinks, so at least some layers retain direct long-range access

slides.title: When Not to Reach for It
slides.body: Sliding window attention is a serving-cost optimization, not a free upgrade — it trades something real for the savings.
bullets: If your task genuinely needs exact recall of arbitrary far-back tokens (legal contract cross-references, long codebase lookups), pure local windows will lose information the model never gets a chance to re-derive
Shrinking the window saves more compute but narrows the local context the model reasons over at each step — there's a real accuracy/cost tradeoff, not just a free lunch
For short sequences (well under the window size), sliding window attention behaves identically to full attention — there's no benefit to adding it
It composes with, but doesn't replace, other long-context tricks: PagedAttention manages how the cache is stored in memory; sliding window changes what's stored in the first place

slides.title: Bound the Window, Bound the Cost
bullets: Sliding window attention caps each token's attention span to the last W tokens, cutting per-layer cost from quadratic to roughly linear in sequence length
Stacking layers lets the effective range grow past W, but exact recall of very distant tokens isn't guaranteed through multi-hop propagation alone
Production models (e.g. Mistral 7B) mix sliding-window layers with periodic full-attention layers to keep both the cost savings and a path to long-range context
Pick it when sequences are long and dependencies are mostly local (chat, code); be cautious when the task demands exact recall of arbitrary far-back facts

questions.prompt: What does sliding window attention change about standard self-attention?
options: It removes attention entirely and replaces it with convolutions
Each token only attends to a fixed-size window of nearby tokens instead of the entire preceding sequence
It only works during training, not inference
It increases the KV cache size to improve accuracy
questions.explanation: By capping attention to the last W tokens, both the per-layer compute and the per-layer KV cache size stop scaling with the full sequence length.

questions.prompt: Why can a sliding-window model still sometimes access information beyond one layer's window?
options: It can't — information outside the window is permanently lost
Stacking multiple sliding-window layers lets the effective receptive field grow to roughly L×W, similar to stacked convolutions
The window size doubles automatically at inference time
Global attention is always run as a backup on every token
questions.explanation: Each layer's output feeds the next layer's input, so information can hop forward across layers — but this is an indirect, lossier path compared to a dedicated full-attention layer.

questions.prompt: Why do models like Mistral 7B interleave full-attention layers with sliding-window layers instead of using sliding windows everywhere?
options: Full-attention layers are cheaper to compute
Pure sliding-window attention can miss exact recall of facts far outside the window, so periodic full-attention layers patch that gap
Interleaving layers is required by hardware, not a design choice
Sliding window attention doesn't work with transformers at all
questions.explanation: A fact that sits far outside every layer's local window has no direct attention path to a token generated much later — mixing in full-attention layers keeps at least some long-range connections intact.

posts.title: Orchard: Microsoft Opens Up Its Agent-Training Stack
posts.subtitle: A Kubernetes-based sandbox service plus three recipes turn a 3B model into a 73%-on-SWE-bench coding agent
posts.summary: Microsoft Research open-sourced Orchard, a Kubernetes-based environment service plus three training recipes (SWE, GUI, personal-assistant agents) for building agentic AI without proprietary sandboxes. Its SWE recipe pushes a small, same-size-for-two-years model from 61.4% to about 73% on SWE-bench Verified using credit-assignment fine-tuning, a sparse-reward RL method, and inference-time reranking.

slides.title: Frontier Agent Training Has Been a Walled Garden — Until Now
slides.body: Microsoft Research released Orchard: an open framework for training agentic AI, including the sandboxing infrastructure and the training recipes that labs normally keep private.
bullets: Published Aug 3, 2026 on the Microsoft Research blog
Ships code, training data, and 3 domain recipes: coding, browser GUI, personal assistant
Its coding recipe lifts a model from 61.4% to ~73% on SWE-bench Verified

slides.title: You Can't Reproduce What You Can't See
slides.body: Strong agentic systems depend on three things most researchers never get access to.
bullets: Proprietary sandboxes to safely run thousands of parallel agent rollouts
Closed RL training pipelines tuned for sparse, delayed success signals
Private datasets of real agent-harness trajectories

slides.title: Orchard Env: Thousands of Disposable Sandboxes on Kubernetes
slides.body: Orchard Env is a standalone service decoupled from any single training framework.
bullets: Creates, manages, and tears down thousands of isolated containers in parallel
A lightweight proxy records real model calls made inside an actual agent harness (Codex, OpenClaw, ZeroClaw)
Each rollout runs inside the exact harness the agent will be deployed in — no train/deploy mismatch

slides.title: Three Recipes Stack Four Distinct Training Tricks
slides.body: Orchard-SWE (coding), Orchard-GUI (browser navigation), and Orchard-Claw (personal-assistant tasks) share a common recipe pattern.
bullets: Credit-assignment SFT: learns from the productive part of a partial, ultimately-failed attempt (107K trajectories distilled from MiniMax-M2.5 and Qwen3.5-397B)
Balanced Adaptive Rollout: an RL method built for sparse, all-or-nothing success signals
Dense-reward shaping: on-policy distillation from a stronger teacher + a process reward model that scores debugging habits, not just the final answer
A 4B-parameter value model, trained on 20 prior experiments' trajectories, reranks candidate solutions at inference time

slides.title: Each Training Stage Buys a Few More Points
slides.body: Microsoft's own numbers show where the gains actually come from — this is a research release, not an independently audited benchmark.
bullets: Orchard-GUI averages 68.4% across WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, and DeepShop
Orchard-Claw under the Codex harness jumps from 18.6% (untrained) to 51.5% after training

slides.title: Worked Example: Why 'Partial Credit' Changes the Training Signal
slides.body: A coding agent that writes a correct patch but fails one edge-case test used to count as a total RL failure — zero signal, no matter how close it got.
bullets: Credit-assignment SFT instead extracts the useful sub-trajectory (correct localization, mostly-right patch) as a positive training example
Balanced Adaptive Rollout then spends more rollout budget near the decision points that actually determine success or failure
Microsoft reports this combination is state of the art among open models near ~3B active parameters, and competitive with systems reported as 10-30x larger

slides.title: Read the Numbers With the Same Report's Own Caveats
slides.body: The post is refreshingly explicit about its own inconsistencies and limits.
bullets: Orchard-SWE's size is reported inconsistently in the same post: ~3B active params in text, '35B-A3B' in one figure caption, '30B-A3B' in the image alt text
The 'competitive with 10x larger systems' claim is stated elsewhere as '10-30x'
This is Microsoft's self-reported research release, not a third-party, independently verified evaluation

slides.title: Why This Matters Beyond One Benchmark Score
bullets: Orchard Env is the reusable piece: a general sandboxing layer any lab could point at a new domain
Training inside the real deployment harness (not a proxy environment) is the architectural bet worth copying
Sparse-reward RL (Balanced Adaptive Rollout) + dense-reward shaping is becoming the standard two-layer recipe for agent RL
Double-check any benchmark claim in a self-reported release against the paper's own figures and captions — this one contradicts itself

questions.prompt: What problem does running each Orchard rollout inside the actual target agent harness (e.g. Codex, OpenClaw) solve?
options: It makes training faster by skipping containers entirely
It removes the mismatch between the environment an agent trains in and the one it's deployed in
It eliminates the need for a reward signal
It lets the model skip tool calls
questions.explanation: A common failure mode in agent RL is training in a simplified proxy environment, then deploying into a real harness with different tool-call formats and constraints. Orchard avoids that by recording trajectories from, and training inside, the real harness.

questions.prompt: Why does Balanced Adaptive Rollout matter for tasks like SWE-bench, where most rollouts simply fail outright?
options: It guarantees every rollout succeeds
It spends more of the rollout budget near the decision points that actually separate success from failure, which is crucial when success signal is sparse
It replaces the reward model with a rule-based checker
It only works on GUI tasks
questions.explanation: Sparse, all-or-nothing rewards make naive RL sample-inefficient — most rollouts carry no gradient signal. Balanced Adaptive Rollout targets compute at the points where outcomes are actually decided.

questions.prompt: According to Microsoft's own reported numbers, what moved Orchard-SWE from 69.7% to roughly 73% on SWE-bench Verified?
options: A larger base model
More training data only
A 4B-parameter value model reranking candidate solutions at inference time
Switching from Codex to ZeroClaw
questions.explanation: The final gain came from inference-time reranking: a separate value model, trained on trajectories from 20 prior experiments, scores and picks among candidate solutions rather than changing the base policy itself.
