posts.title: Knowledge Distillation: Teaching a Small Model to Think Like a Big One
posts.subtitle: Why the probabilities a giant model assigns to its wrong answers are worth more than the one label it gets right.
posts.summary: Knowledge distillation trains a small 'student' model to reproduce a large 'teacher' model's behavior — not by copying weights, but by learning from the teacher's own outputs. It's the default recipe behind most fast, cheap model variants you use today, and it comes with real tradeoffs: inherited blind spots, lost long-tail knowledge, and safety behavior that doesn't transfer for free.

slides.title: You Can't Ship a 70B-Parameter Model to a Phone — But You Can Ship Its Judgment
slides.body: Knowledge distillation trains a small, fast 'student' model to mimic a large 'teacher' model's behavior, so you get most of the teacher's quality at a fraction of the compute.

slides.title: Scale Helps at Training Time — and Hurts at Serving Time
bullets: A frontier-scale model needs multiple GPUs just to hold its weights in memory, which makes every inference call expensive and slow.
Training a small model from scratch on the same raw dataset rarely matches the large model's quality — a lot of a big model's capability comes from scale itself, not just data.
Most products don't need the full model's breadth — they need reliably good performance on a narrower task, fast and cheap, at massive request volume.

slides.title: The Student Learns From the Teacher's Probabilities, Not Just Its Final Answer
slides.body: Classic distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) trains the student to match the teacher's full output distribution — 'soft labels' — not just whichever single answer scored highest.
bullets: Soft targets carry 'dark knowledge': the relative probability the teacher puts on every wrong answer, not just its top pick.
A 'temperature' parameter softens the teacher's distribution during distillation, so small probability differences between wrong answers become learnable signal instead of rounding to zero.
Modern LLM distillation often skips raw logits entirely: generate many teacher completions and fine-tune the student directly on that synthetic text — 'sequence-level' distillation.

slides.title: Distillation in the Wild: DistilBERT's Numbers

rows: ~40% fewer parameters, ~60% faster inference, retains ~97% of BERT's language-understanding performance
Sequence-level: fine-tune on large volumes of a bigger sibling model's generated completions
Much cheaper to serve; gap to the teacher narrows on the tasks that dominate the synthetic training data, widens elsewhere

slides.title: Worked Example: Building a Support Classifier Without a Teacher-Sized GPU Bill
bullets: Step 1: Run 50,000 real support tickets through the large teacher model, saving both its answer and its confidence distribution over categories.
Step 2: Train a student model with a few hundred million parameters on those (ticket, soft-label) pairs instead of on hand-labeled data alone.
Step 3: Deploy the student — it fits on a single commodity GPU (or even CPU) and answers in milliseconds instead of seconds.
Result: most of the teacher's accuracy on this specific, narrow task, at a small fraction of the serving cost — because the student only had to learn one job, not everything the teacher knows.

slides.title: Distillation Isn't Free: What You Give Up
bullets: The student inherits the teacher's blind spots — if the teacher is confidently wrong, the student learns to be confidently wrong the same way.
Students typically lose ground on tasks needing broad world knowledge or long-tail reasoning they never saw enough signal for during distillation.

Safety and refusal behavior don't transfer automatically — a student trained only on a teacher's raw outputs can lack the teacher's guardrails unless that behavior is explicitly part of the training data.

It's also a live industry flashpoint: in 2026, labs including Anthropic have accused rivals of large-scale, unauthorized distillation of their frontier models' API outputs — treating it as a terms-of-service and export-control issue, not just a training technique.

slides.title: The Core Idea, in One Line
slides.body: Distillation transfers behavior through training signal generated by a stronger model — it's a recipe for making models smaller and faster, not a way to make them smarter than their teacher.
bullets: If you've used a fast, cheap 'mini' or 'lite' version of a flagship LLM, there's a good chance distillation is part of why it exists.

questions.prompt: In classic knowledge distillation, what is 'dark knowledge'?
options: Hidden internal weights only the teacher model can access
The information carried in the relative probabilities a teacher assigns to its wrong answers, not just its top pick
An encrypted copy of the teacher's parameters
A set of adversarial examples used to attack the student
questions.explanation: A teacher that's 90% confident in 'cat' but puts 8% on 'dog' and 0.001% on 'car' is telling the student something about similarity structure that a hard 0/1 label never reveals — that extra signal in the wrong-answer probabilities is the 'dark knowledge.'

questions.prompt: Why does raising the 'temperature' of the softmax matter during distillation?
options: It speeds up the student's training loop
It softens the teacher's probability distribution so small differences between wrong answers become learnable signal instead of rounding to near-zero
It reduces the student model's parameter count
It prevents the teacher model from overfitting
questions.explanation: Without temperature scaling, a confident teacher's output distribution is nearly all weight on one answer and near-zero everywhere else, which gives the student almost nothing to learn from beyond the hard label. A higher temperature spreads that distribution out so the 'dark knowledge' becomes usable.

questions.prompt: What's a real risk a distilled student model inherits from its teacher?
options: Distilled models always end up larger than their teacher over time
The student inherits the teacher's blind spots and biases, and may lack the teacher's safety/refusal training unless that's explicitly included in the training data
Distilled models become more expensive to run than the original teacher
The student automatically gains knowledge the teacher never had
questions.explanation: Because the student learns only from the teacher's outputs (or synthetic text generated from them), it reproduces whatever the teacher gets confidently wrong — and unless safety behavior is explicitly part of that training signal, it isn't guaranteed to carry over.

posts.title: StudentSim: Teaching AI Tutors by Simulating the Student
posts.subtitle: Microsoft builds a personalized AI double of each learner so tutor models can rehearse before ever meeting a human.
posts.summary: StudentSim trains personalized simulators of individual students so AI tutors can be tested and RL-trained without costly real-learner studies. On a chess benchmark, tutors trained against StudentSim rewards beat GPT-5.4-reward and no-RL baselines by double digits on human-expert ratings.

slides.title: What If You Could Rehearse Teaching Before Meeting the Student?
slides.body: Microsoft Research built StudentSim: an AI system that models exactly how one real learner answers — and how that answer changes after a tutor steps in.

slides.title: Real-Student Testing Is Too Slow to Keep Up With Model Iteration
bullets: Tutor quality isn't about the guidance itself — it's about what the student does after reading it.
Running that loop with real learners for every model update is slow, expensive, and hard to repeat.
Without fast feedback, teams can't tell if a new tutor prompt actually helps anyone learn.

slides.title: Two-Stage Training Builds a Simulator of One Specific Learner
slides.body: StudentSim first trains on records pooled across many students in a domain to learn common error patterns, then specializes on a single student's own sparse records.
bullets: Stage 1: learn generic mistake patterns from pooled, de-identified public datasets.
Stage 2: fine-tune on one learner's own history, even when that history is thin.
Only publicly released, de-identified research datasets are used — no PII.

slides.title: StudentSimEval Scores Two Different Things, Not Just Accuracy
slides.body: The benchmark spans chess, second-language English writing, and math, and borrows from Vygotsky's zone of proximal development.
bullets: Behavioral fidelity: does the simulator match this student's real answers on held-out problems?
Guidance responsiveness: does the simulator's answer actually change after reading tutor guidance?
A good tutoring simulator needs both — matching the student alone isn't enough if it never learns.

slides.title: StudentSim Beats General LLMs at Matching a Specific Learner
A Frozen Simulator Becomes the Reward Signal for Tutor RL
slides.body: In a chess study, a personalized StudentSim is frozen and used purely to grade tutors: it reads the tutor's guidance, revises the student's move, and Stockfish scores the improvement.
bullets: Tutor trained with StudentSim-based RL reward: 90.5% accuracy per blind human chess-expert review.
No-RL baseline tutor: 75.7% accuracy on the same blind review.
Tutor trained with a GPT-5.4-based reward instead: only 71.6% — worse than no RL at all.
Experts also rated the StudentSim-trained tutor highest on guidance quality and personalization.

slides.title: A Research Tool, Not a Classroom Replacement — Know the Limits
slides.body: Microsoft is explicit: StudentSim is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and does not replace teachers.
bullets: Pitfall: matching past answers doesn't guarantee the simulator predicts real learning outcomes.
Human studies are still required for safety, usability, and classroom fit before any real deployment.
Only validated on three domains so far (chess, L2 writing, math) — generalization elsewhere is untested.
Takeaway: simulate learners to iterate fast on tutor design, then validate the winner with real students.

questions.prompt: Why does StudentSim need a two-stage training process instead of just prompting a general model like GPT-5.4?
options: It's cheaper to run at inference time
Pooled training learns general error patterns, then per-student fine-tuning matches one learner's specific (and often sparse) history
GPT-5.4 cannot process chess positions
Two-stage training removes the need for any evaluation benchmark
questions.explanation: The results show why this matters: GPT-5.4 responds to guidance reasonably (0.7186) but matches a specific student's actual behavior poorly (0.2316) — it hasn't specialized to that one learner's patterns the way the two-stage approach does.

questions.prompt: In the chess tutor RL experiment, what provided the reward signal for training the tutor?
options: Direct human ratings during training
A fixed rule-based scoring table
Stockfish's evaluation of how much the student's revised move improved after reading tutor guidance
The tutor's own confidence score
questions.explanation: A frozen personalized StudentSim reads the tutor's guidance and revises the student's move; Stockfish then scores the quality improvement, and that improvement becomes the RL reward — letting the tutor be trained without a human in the loop for every step.

questions.prompt: What limitation does Microsoft Research explicitly flag about StudentSim?
options: It only works for English-language students
It requires expensive proprietary data
It is a research tool, not deployed in classrooms, and still requires real human studies before any real-world use
It cannot be evaluated on held-out data
questions.explanation: The authors are careful to frame this as a proof of concept: good fidelity to past answers doesn't guarantee the simulator captures real learning outcomes, safety, or usability — those still need actual student studies.

references.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring — Microsoft Research Blog
StudentSim: Training LLM-Based Student Simulators — Microsoft Research Publication

posts.title: Attention Sinks: Why LLMs Hoard the First Few Tokens
posts.subtitle: Evict the start of a long conversation from the cache and a streaming LLM falls apart — here's the trick that keeps it stable forever.
posts.summary: A sliding-window KV cache should let an LLM run forever on a fixed memory budget, but naively evicting the earliest tokens causes the model to break down. The fix: permanently pin a handful of 'sink' tokens, because the attention mechanism uses them as a dumping ground for leftover probability mass it has nowhere else to put.

slides.title: The Most Important Tokens in a Long Chat Are Often Meaningless
slides.body: A streaming LLM that evicts its very first few tokens from memory doesn't just forget them — it falls apart. The reason has nothing to do with what those tokens say.

slides.title: A Plain Sliding Window Collapses the Moment It Fills Up
slides.body: To serve a conversation of unbounded length, you can't keep every token's key/value vectors forever — memory would grow without limit. The obvious fix is a fixed-size sliding window that drops the oldest tokens.
bullets: Works fine while the window hasn't filled — looks like a free lunch.
The instant the very first tokens get evicted, generation quality collapses: fluency breaks down and outputs degrade into repetition or incoherence.
This happens even though those first tokens (often just a beginning-of-sequence marker) carry almost no semantic content.

slides.title: Softmax Always Sums to 1 — Even When Nothing Is Relevant
slides.body: Attention is a softmax over all visible tokens, so it must distribute 100% of its weight every single step, even at positions where no token is actually a good match for the current query.
bullets: The model needs somewhere to dump that unavoidable leftover probability mass.
Because the first few tokens are present at every single position during pretraining, the model learns to route the surplus there by default — regardless of their content.
Those tokens become 'attention sinks': high attention score, low information value.

slides.title: Pin a Handful of Sink Tokens, Slide the Rest
slides.body: Keep the first few tokens' KV pairs permanently in the cache, no matter how long the conversation runs, and slide a normal recency window behind them.
bullets: Just a small fixed number of sink tokens (not a large reserved block) is enough to restore stability.
The rest of the cache behaves like an ordinary sliding window, so total memory stays bounded.
This requires no retraining or fine-tuning — it works on models already trained with a BOS-like token at position zero.

slides.title: Three Ways to Bound KV Cache Memory

rows: Collapses once the first tokens are evicted

slides.title: A Support Bot That Runs for Weeks Without Falling Apart
slides.body: Picture a customer-support assistant kept open across a long back-and-forth, serving with a fixed-size KV cache to control memory cost.
bullets: With a plain sliding window: once the original system prompt's tokens scroll out of the cache, the bot suddenly loses its formatting rules and starts repeating itself.
With sink tokens pinned: the same bot stays coherent indefinitely, because the attention mechanism still has its usual 'release valve' even after the real system-prompt content is long gone.
The fix costs almost nothing — a few extra cached positions versus the alternative of unbounded memory growth.

slides.title: Sinks Buy Stability, Not Memory — Know the Difference
slides.body: Attention sinks solve a specific failure mode: generation collapse from naive eviction. They do not solve recall.
bullets: Pitfall: a model with sink tokens still cannot recall specific facts that have already slid out of its sliding window — it stays fluent, not omniscient.
For tasks needing long-range factual recall, pair this with real long-context handling or retrieval, not sinks alone.
More sink tokens past a small handful give diminishing returns — this is a cheap stabilizer, not a capacity upgrade.
Takeaway: when you need bounded memory and indefinite runtime, pin a few sink tokens behind your sliding window instead of relying on eviction alone.

questions.prompt: Why do the very first tokens in a sequence end up receiving disproportionate attention, even when they carry little real meaning?
options: They are always the longest tokens in the sequence
Softmax attention must distribute all of its probability mass every step, and the model learns to dump leftover mass on tokens present at every position (like the first one)
The tokenizer assigns them a special high-priority embedding
They are duplicated internally by the attention mechanism
questions.explanation: Because softmax always sums to 1, the model needs somewhere to send attention weight when no token is truly relevant. Tokens that appear at the start of every sequence during training become the learned destination for that surplus.

questions.prompt: What specifically breaks when a plain fixed-size sliding window evicts the earliest tokens from the KV cache?
options: Nothing — eviction is always safe once the window is full
Only the model's memory of early facts is lost, with no effect on fluency
Generation quality collapses — the model loses its usual attention 'release valve' and outputs degrade or repeat
The model automatically switches to a larger context window
questions.explanation: The collapse isn't about losing information content — it's that the model's attention mechanism loses the low-information tokens it relies on to absorb excess probability mass, which destabilizes generation.

questions.prompt: What problem do attention sinks explicitly NOT solve?
options: Bounding KV cache memory for long-running generation
Keeping generation fluent and coherent indefinitely
Recalling specific facts or content that have already been evicted from the sliding window
Running inference without retraining the model
questions.explanation: Sink tokens stabilize generation but don't restore evicted information — a system that needs to recall specific facts from far back in a conversation still needs real long-context handling or retrieval, not sinks alone.

posts.title: A2A: The Protocol for Agents Talking to Agents
posts.subtitle: MCP connects an agent to its tools. A2A connects agents to each other.
posts.summary: Agent2Agent (A2A) is an open, JSON-RPC-based protocol — backed by Google and now hosted by the Linux Foundation — that lets independently built AI agents discover each other's capabilities via an Agent Card and hand off stateful, long-running Tasks without exposing their internal memory or tools. It complements MCP: MCP wires an agent to tools, A2A wires agents to other agents.

slides.title: Your agents can use tools. Can they use each other?
slides.body: A2A (Agent2Agent) is an open protocol for letting opaque, independently-built agents discover, delegate to, and collaborate with one another — without either side seeing the other's internals.
bullets: Open-sourced by Google, now under the Linux Foundation, Apache 2.0
SDKs in Python, Go, JavaScript, Java, .NET, Rust
Designed to complement MCP, not replace it

slides.title: MCP solved agent-to-tool. Agent-to-agent was still a mess.
slides.body: Model Context Protocol standardized how one agent calls a tool or data source. But it says nothing about how a LangGraph agent asks a CrewAI agent — running on someone else's server, in someone else's stack — to do a sub-task for it.
bullets: Before A2A: every cross-framework handoff needed custom glue code
Agents are 'opaque' — you can't just read their memory or call their internal functions like a library
A real handoff can take minutes or hours, so a single request/response call isn't enough

slides.title: Four building blocks: Card, Message, Task, Artifact
slides.body: A2A runs JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP(S) and defines just enough structure to let strangers' agents cooperate.
bullets: Agent Card — a JSON manifest at /.well-known/agent-card.json listing an agent's skills, endpoint, and auth requirements
Message — one turn of dialogue (role: user|agent) built from Parts: text, structured data, or a file/URL
Task — a stateful unit of work with a unique ID; related tasks share a server-issued contextId
Artifact — the tangible output of a task (a document, image, JSON blob), streamable in increments

slides.title: Worked example: an orchestrator delegates a booking
slides.body: A trip-planning agent needs to book a flight but has no booking logic of its own.
bullets: 1. It fetches GET /.well-known/agent-card.json from a flight-booking agent's domain to see what it can do
2. It sends a Message naming the route and dates — the server replies with a new Task in an active state
3. The booking agent needs the traveler's seat preference → Task moves to input-required; orchestrator sends another Message to answer
4. Booking confirmed → Task reaches the terminal state completed, carrying an Artifact (the e-ticket JSON)
If the fare expires first, the Task instead ends in failed or canceled — never silently stuck

slides.title: A2A vs. MCP: different layers, same stack
slides.body: They're frequently paired: an orchestrator agent might use A2A to delegate to a specialist agent, which then uses MCP to call its own tools.

rows: A Task — stateful, can run long and multi-turn
Only a capability summary (Agent Card); internals stay opaque
JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP(S), plus SSE streaming and async push

slides.title: When A2A is overkill
slides.body: A2A is built for cross-boundary delegation between separately-owned agents. It's the wrong tool for a lot of agentic code.
bullets: Calling your own sub-agent in-process? Just call the function — don't wrap it in a network protocol
Need an agent to use a calculator, a database, or a search API? That's a tool call — reach for MCP, not A2A
Every Agent Card and Task state is a new attack surface: a malicious agent can advertise a Card it doesn't honor, so auth and capability checks still matter
The spec is young — expect auth schemes in Agent Cards and push-notification reliability to keep evolving

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: A2A lets agents built on different frameworks discover and delegate to each other over plain JSON-RPC
Agent Cards (at a well-known URL) advertise capabilities; Tasks track long-running, multi-turn work to a terminal state
MCP = agent-to-tool. A2A = agent-to-agent. Most serious multi-agent systems will end up using both
Reach for it only at a real organizational or framework boundary — not as a replacement for an in-process function call

questions.prompt: What gap does A2A fill that MCP does not?
options: Letting one agent call a database or search tool
Letting independently-built agents discover each other and delegate stateful work without exposing internals
Compressing an LLM's KV cache
Formatting prompts for few-shot learning
questions.explanation: MCP standardizes agent-to-tool calls. A2A standardizes agent-to-agent collaboration — discovery via Agent Cards and delegation via Tasks — between agents that may be on entirely different frameworks and servers.

questions.prompt: Where does a client look by default to learn what an A2A agent can do?
options: A hardcoded config file shipped with the client
An email to the agent's maintainer
/.well-known/agent-card.json on the agent's domain
The agent's GitHub README
questions.explanation: A2A defines a standard discovery path, https://{domain}/.well-known/agent-card.json (following RFC 8615), that serves a JSON Agent Card describing skills, endpoint, and auth requirements.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a terminal state for an A2A Task?
options: input-required
auth-required
completed
streaming
questions.explanation: completed is terminal, along with canceled, failed, and rejected. input-required and auth-required are interrupted states — the task is paused waiting on the client, not finished.

references.title: A2A Protocol — official specification and SDKs (a2aproject/A2A)

posts.title: H-JEPA: Planning Gets Easier When the World Model Has Levels
posts.subtitle: Stack three JEPA world models on top of each other and AntMaze success jumps from 18% to 73%.
posts.summary: H-JEPA stacks several JEPA-style world models, each predicting further into the future in its own coarser latent space, so planning can happen top-down: pick a rough subgoal, then refine it level by level. On the Visual AntMaze benchmark a three-level hierarchy raises planning success from 18% to 73% versus a flat world model, while using less planner compute, and the same recipe extends to real-robot video from DROID.

slides.title: One world model, one timescale — that's the bottleneck
slides.body: Latent world models like JEPA learn to predict what a scene will look like next, then let an agent plan by imagining action sequences inside that learned space. But a single flat model has to represent every timescale at once — the next frame and the next five minutes — in the same latent space.
bullets: Paper: H-JEPA: End-to-End Learning of Hierarchical World Models for Visual Planning (Zhang, Terver, Rabbat, LeCun, Balestriero)
Builds on LeWM, the same group's flat latent world model baseline

slides.title: Long-horizon planning explodes in a flat latent space
slides.body: To plan 100 steps ahead, a flat world model has to simulate roughly 100 latent transitions, and errors compound at every step. It also can't tell the difference between fast, unpredictable pixel-level detail and the slow, task-relevant state that actually matters for the goal.
bullets: Planning cost scales roughly with the number of raw timesteps simulated
Fine-grained detail (lighting, texture) gets mixed into the same latent as coarse task state (position, contact)
Compounding prediction error makes long rollouts unreliable

slides.title: Stack JEPA models, one per timescale
slides.body: H-JEPA trains a hierarchy of action-conditioned JEPA predictors end-to-end. Each level predicts further ahead in time than the level below it, in its own, coarser latent space that drops fast, unpredictable detail and keeps only what's relevant at that timescale.
bullets: Level N (top): coarsest latent, longest jump — predicts 'where should we roughly be'
Level 1 (bottom): finest latent, shortest jump — predicts next-step dynamics for low-level control
Trained end-to-end rather than level-by-level, so levels learn representations that compose

slides.title: Planning runs top-down
slides.body: At inference, planning starts at the top level: search over coarse latent trajectories to pick a long-horizon subgoal. That subgoal becomes the target for the level below, which plans a finer path toward it — and so on down to the bottom level, which outputs the next action.
bullets: Each level only has to plan over a handful of its own coarse steps, not hundreds of raw steps
Subgoals from a higher level constrain and shrink the search space for the level below
Lower planner compute per query than searching the full horizon in one flat latent space

slides.title: Visual AntMaze: 18% to 73%
slides.body: The headline benchmark is Visual AntMaze, a long-horizon navigation task from pixels. Ablations attribute the gain to both the temporal decomposition (each level handling its own timescale) and the higher-level goal representations acting as useful subgoals.

slides.title: Worked example: crossing a multi-room maze
slides.body: Imagine AntMaze as three connected rooms with a goal in the far room. A flat model must simulate every intermediate step to evaluate a full path. H-JEPA's top level instead reasons directly in 'which room next' terms.
bullets: Top level: picks 'go to room 2, then room 3' as a coarse subgoal sequence
Mid level: plans a rough path across room 2 toward its exit
Bottom level: outputs the actual joint torques to move the ant one step along that path
The same recipe transfers to real-robot video from the DROID dataset using inverse-dynamics supervision, improving offline planning fidelity at lower planner compute

slides.title: Where the hierarchy doesn't help — or adds cost
slides.body: Hierarchy is not free: it adds design choices and failure modes that a flat world model doesn't have.
bullets: More hyperparameters: number of levels and the timescale ratio between them must be tuned per task
On short-horizon tasks like FourRoom and Push-T, the paper reports the hierarchy performs similarly to the flat baseline — the AntMaze-style long-horizon gain doesn't universally apply
If a higher level picks an infeasible subgoal, errors cascade downward just like compounding error in a flat model, only now across levels instead of timesteps
End-to-end training of multiple stacked levels is more complex to get stable than training one flat model

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: H-JEPA stacks action-conditioned JEPA world models, each predicting farther ahead in its own coarser latent space
Planning goes top-down: coarse subgoals from higher levels constrain the search at lower levels
On Visual AntMaze, 3 levels take success from ~18% to ~73% while lowering planner compute
The gain is largest on long-horizon tasks; on short-horizon tasks the hierarchy doesn't clearly beat a flat model
The same hierarchical recipe extends to real-robot video (DROID) via inverse-dynamics supervision

questions.prompt: What does each level of H-JEPA's hierarchy predict differently from the level below it?
options: The same thing, just with more parameters
Further ahead in time, in its own coarser latent space that drops fast, unpredictable detail
A different input modality, like audio instead of video
Nothing — all levels share one latent space
questions.explanation: Each level predicts a longer jump into the future than the level below it, and does so in a coarser latent space tuned to that timescale — dropping fine detail that's irrelevant at that level and keeping only what matters for planning at that horizon.

questions.prompt: Why does H-JEPA need less planner compute than a flat world model on long-horizon tasks?
options: It uses a smaller neural network overall
It skips verification entirely
Higher levels pick coarse subgoals that shrink the search space each lower level has to explore
It only plans one step ahead at every level
questions.explanation: Instead of searching the full horizon in one flat latent space, each level only has to plan over its own handful of coarse steps, guided by the subgoal handed down from the level above — so the total search is much smaller than simulating every raw timestep.

questions.prompt: According to the paper, where does the 3-level hierarchy NOT clearly beat the flat baseline?
options: On Visual AntMaze, a long-horizon navigation task
On short-horizon tasks like FourRoom Distractors and Push-T
On real-robot video from DROID
It beats the flat baseline everywhere by a wide margin
questions.explanation: The paper reports the hierarchy's advantage is largest on long-horizon tasks like AntMaze; on short-horizon tasks such as FourRoom and Push-T, hierarchical and flat planning perform similarly, since there's less long-range structure for the hierarchy to exploit.

references.title: H-JEPA: End-to-End Learning of Hierarchical World Models for Visual Planning (arXiv:2610.06805)

posts.title: Kandinsky 6.0: Open Video That Generates Its Own Lip-Synced Audio
posts.subtitle: A 29B diffusion model trains video and audio together, so the sound comes out already in sync.
posts.summary: Kandinsky Lab open-sourced Kandinsky 6.0 Video, an MIT-licensed family of diffusion models (3B Lite and 29B Pro) that generate 5-second clips with synchronized 44 kHz audio from text or an image-plus-text prompt, plus a separate super-resolution model that upscales output to Full HD.

slides.title: Most open video generators are silent
slides.body: Kandinsky 6.0 Video, released by Kandinsky Lab on October 6, 2026, generates video and audio from one joint diffusion process instead of bolting sound on afterward — so mouth movements and sound events land in sync by construction.
bullets: Open weights, MIT license, available day-one in Diffusers, ComfyUI, vLLM-Omni, SGLang, and FastVideo
Two sizes: 3B Lite and 29B Pro, both text-to-audio-video and image-to-audio-video

slides.title: Bolted-on audio rarely lines up
slides.body: The common pipeline is: generate silent video, then generate or retrieve audio separately, then try to align the two. Mouth shapes drift out of sync with speech, and sound effects (a door slamming, a string being plucked) land a few frames off from the visual event.
bullets: Two separate generation steps means two separate sources of timing error
Post-hoc alignment can't fix content the audio model never saw happen on screen

slides.title: One diffusion process, two streams, cross-attention between them
slides.body: The audio stream is trained first on its own, then both the video and audio streams are trained jointly on paired audio-video data with bidirectional cross-attention linking them, followed by supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement-learning post-training, and distillation.
bullets: Because both streams denoise together and attend to each other, audio timing is learned jointly with motion, not fitted afterward
Every generation ships as a 5-second clip with 44 kHz audio out of the same model
A separate super-resolution model upscales the result to Full HD (1920x1080)

slides.title: From prompt to final clip
slides.body: A text (or image+text) prompt feeds the joint video-audio diffusion model, producing a base-resolution synchronized clip. For faster iteration, a 10-step distilled checkpoint trades some quality for much shorter generation time; the separate VSR model is a later, optional pass.
bullets: Input: text prompt, or an image plus text for image-to-audio-video
Core: joint diffusion over video + audio latents with cross-attention
Optional: 10-step distilled checkpoint for speed, or the full (non-distilled) checkpoint for quality
Optional: Kandinsky 6.0 VSR pass to reach Full HD

slides.title: What a 5-second clip actually costs you in time
slides.body: The official repo publishes generation-time benchmarks (excluding weight loading and video encoding) for the non-distilled checkpoints — there's a real hardware tax for the larger Pro model.

slides.title: Worked example: animating a still photo
slides.body: Image-to-audio-video (TI2AV) takes a single photo of a street musician plus the prompt 'the musician strums the guitar and starts singing' and produces a 5-second clip where the strumming motion, string sound, and vocal audio all land on the same frames.
bullets: Input: one static image + short text description of the action
Output: 5 seconds of motion with 44 kHz audio generated in the same pass
No separate audio model, no manual alignment step

slides.title: Where this isn't the right tool
slides.body: The clip length, hardware cost, and lack of published quality benchmarks matter before reaching for this model.
bullets: Fixed ~5-second clip length — not suited to longer continuous shots without stitching
The 29B Pro model at Full HD takes 6.5–20+ minutes per clip even on an H100 — not viable for real-time or interactive use

The official README ships speed benchmarks but no quality comparisons against competing video-audio models — treat 'competitive with leading models' claims as a vendor claim, not an independent benchmark
The 3B Lite model is the practical choice for fast iteration; reserve 29B Pro for final renders

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Kandinsky 6.0 Video generates video and 44 kHz audio together from one joint diffusion model, so sync comes for free
Two open, MIT-licensed sizes: 3B Lite (fast) and 29B Pro (higher quality, much slower)
A separate super-resolution model handles the Full HD upscale step
Generation time is substantial — minutes per 5-second clip, even on an H100 — so plan for offline rendering, not live use
No independent quality benchmarks are published yet; the official repo only documents speed

questions.prompt: Why is Kandinsky 6.0 Video's audio better synced than a typical 'video then audio' pipeline?
options: It uses a higher sample rate than other models
A human manually aligns the tracks after generation
Video and audio are denoised jointly in one diffusion process with cross-attention between the two streams
It only generates silent video and no audio at all
questions.explanation: Because the video and audio streams attend to each other during the same joint diffusion process, timing is learned together rather than fitted after the fact — which is why mouth movements and sound events land in sync by construction.

questions.prompt: Based on the published generation-time benchmarks, which setup is best suited to fast iteration?
options: 29B Pro at Full HD on an RTX 4090
3B Lite, since it generates a clip in well under a minute's worth of H100 time compared to Pro's Full HD pass
They all take the same amount of time regardless of model size
29B Pro, because larger models are always faster to sample
questions.explanation: The repo's own numbers show the 3B Lite model finishing a clip in roughly 239s on an H100, far faster than the 29B Pro model's ~402s (and much longer on weaker GPUs) — making Lite the practical pick when iterating quickly.

questions.prompt: What should you NOT assume from Kandinsky Lab's claim that Pro is 'competitive with leading audio-video models'?
options: That it has been verified by an independent, third-party benchmark
That the model is open source
That it uses MIT licensing
That it supports both text-to-video and image-to-video
questions.explanation: The official repository publishes generation-speed benchmarks but no head-to-head quality benchmarks against competing models — so a 'competitive with leading models' claim should be treated as a vendor statement until independently verified.

posts.title: LoRA: Fine-Tuning a Giant Model by Training a Tiny Sliver of It
posts.subtitle: Freeze the original weights, learn two small matrices, and adapt a 70B model for the storage cost of a few MB.
posts.summary: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tunes a large model by freezing its original weight matrices and training only a pair of small low-rank matrices whose product approximates the needed weight update. This cuts trainable parameters by 100-1000x, shrinks per-task storage to a few megabytes, and lets you swap fine-tuned 'adapters' in and out of one frozen base model at inference time.

slides.title: You don't need to touch all 70 billion parameters to adapt a model
slides.body: Full fine-tuning updates every weight in a model and needs memory for gradients and optimizer state on top of the weights themselves — often 3-4x the model's size. LoRA gets most of the benefit by training a tiny add-on instead of the model itself.
bullets: Introduced by Hu et al. (2021), now the default way to fine-tune LLMs and diffusion models cheaply
Original weights stay completely frozen during training

slides.title: Full fine-tuning is expensive to train AND to keep around
slides.body: Training needs memory for the weights, the gradients, and the optimizer state (e.g. Adam keeps two extra numbers per parameter) — for a 70B model that's well beyond a single high-end GPU. And once trained, every task needs its own full copy of the model to store and serve.
bullets: Optimizer state alone can be 2x the parameter count for Adam-style optimizers
Ten fine-tuned variants of a 70B model means ten full 70B-parameter copies on disk
Switching between tasks at serving time means swapping entire multi-gigabyte models

slides.title: Decompose the update into two small matrices
slides.body: For a frozen weight matrix W (size d x k), LoRA represents the fine-tuning update as the product of two much smaller matrices: A (d x r) and B (r x k), where the rank r is tiny compared to d and k — typically 4 to 64. Only A and B are trained; W never changes.
bullets: The forward pass becomes h = Wx + (alpha/r) * B(Ax), where alpha is a fixed scaling hyperparameter
A is usually initialized to zero or small random values, B to zero, so training starts as a no-op
Lower rank r means fewer trainable parameters, but less capacity to represent a complex update

slides.title: At inference: merge it in, or keep it swappable
slides.body: LoRA is typically applied to the attention and MLP projection matrices inside each transformer layer, not to embeddings. At serving time you have two options with very different tradeoffs.
bullets: Merge: compute W' = W + (alpha/r)*BA once, bake it into the weights — zero extra inference latency, but loses the ability to swap adapters
Keep separate: store W frozen and B·A as a small adapter — lets you hot-swap different task adapters onto the same base model, at the cost of one extra matrix multiply per forward pass
A handful of megabytes per adapter vs. tens of gigabytes per full fine-tuned model

slides.title: Full fine-tuning vs. LoRA, concretely
Worked example: one 4096x4096 weight matrix
slides.body: A single attention projection matrix of size 4096 x 4096 has about 16.8 million parameters. Fine-tuning it fully means training all 16.8M of them.
bullets: With LoRA at rank r=8: A is 4096x8 and B is 8x4096, together 2 x (4096x8) = 65,536 trainable parameters
That's roughly 0.4% of the original 16.8M — a ~256x reduction for this one matrix
Across a whole 70B model, this adds up to total trainable parameters typically in the tens of millions, not tens of billions

slides.title: When rank, placement, and task complexity bite
slides.body: LoRA's efficiency comes with real tradeoffs that pick the rank and placement matter for.
bullets: Too-low rank underfits tasks that need a large representational shift from the base model (e.g. teaching an entirely new skill, not just a style)
Too-high rank erodes the memory savings and starts approaching full fine-tuning's cost without a guaranteed accuracy win
Applying LoRA only to attention/MLP projections (the common default) can miss cases where the embedding or output layer needs to change
QLoRA extends the idea to a 4-bit quantized frozen base model, cutting base-model memory further, at some added quantization error
Stacking or merging multiple LoRA adapters on the same base model can cause them to interfere with each other's learned directions

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: LoRA freezes the original weights and trains only two small low-rank matrices, A and B, whose product approximates the fine-tuning update
Rank r controls the tradeoff: lower r means fewer parameters but less capacity to represent a complex update
Per-task storage drops from a full model copy to a few megabytes, enabling cheap, swappable task adapters
Merge the adapter into the weights for zero extra latency, or keep it separate to hot-swap tasks on one base model
QLoRA combines LoRA with a quantized frozen base to fine-tune even larger models on modest hardware

questions.prompt: During LoRA fine-tuning, what happens to the original weight matrix W?
options: It's deleted and replaced entirely by B*A
It's quantized to 4-bit precision
It stays completely frozen; only the small matrices A and B are trained
It's fine-tuned along with A and B, just at a lower learning rate
questions.explanation: LoRA's whole point is to leave the large pretrained weight matrix W untouched and only train the much smaller A and B matrices, whose product approximates the needed update — that's what keeps trainable parameters and memory low.

questions.prompt: A weight matrix has 16.8 million parameters. Using LoRA at rank r=8, roughly how many parameters are actually trained for that matrix?
options: 16.8 million, same as full fine-tuning
About 65,536 — roughly 0.4% of the original
Exactly 8, one per rank dimension
8.4 million, half of the original
questions.explanation: With A sized (d x r) and B sized (r x k), rank r=8 on a 4096x4096 matrix gives 2 x (4096 x 8) = 65,536 trainable parameters — about 0.4% of the 16.8M in the full matrix, which is the source of LoRA's efficiency.

questions.prompt: Why would you choose to keep a LoRA adapter separate from the base model instead of merging it in?
options: Merging always produces worse accuracy
Keeping it separate removes the need for the base model entirely
It lets you hot-swap different task adapters onto the same frozen base model, at the cost of one extra matrix multiply per forward pass
Separate adapters train faster than merged ones
questions.explanation: Merging bakes the adapter into the weights for zero extra inference cost but locks in one task. Keeping B*A separate costs a small extra matrix multiply at inference but lets you swap in a different few-megabyte adapter for a different task without touching the base model.

posts.title: Speculative Decoding: Guessing Tokens to Skip the Wait
posts.subtitle: A small draft model guesses ahead; the big model checks the guesses all at once.
posts.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM text generation by having a small draft model propose several tokens ahead, then letting the large target model verify all of them in a single parallel pass — accepting the correct ones and resampling only where the guess was wrong, with no change to the output distribution.

slides.title: Generating text one token at a time is wasteful
slides.body: A large language model normally generates text autoregressively: run the full model, get one token, append it, run the full model again. Speculative decoding breaks that one-token-per-pass bottleneck without changing a single output token.
bullets: Lossless: the final output is statistically identical to plain decoding
Used in production serving stacks for low-latency chat and coding assistants

slides.title: Decoding is bottlenecked on memory, not math
slides.body: Generating one token means streaming the entire model's weights through the GPU just to produce a single output. The GPU's compute units sit mostly idle, waiting on memory bandwidth — the classic sign of a memory-bound, under-utilized workload.
bullets: Each forward pass reads every weight in the model, for one token
Batch size of 1 means the GPU's matrix units are rarely saturated
More GPUs don't fix this — the bottleneck is bandwidth, not FLOPs

slides.title: Draft cheaply, verify in parallel
slides.body: Pair the big 'target' model with a much smaller, faster 'draft' model (or a lightweight head on the same model). The draft proposes several tokens in a row; the target model checks all of them in one forward pass instead of one-by-one.
bullets: Draft model generates K tokens autoregressively — cheap, since it's small
Target model scores all K draft tokens plus the next one in a single batched pass
One expensive forward pass can now validate multiple tokens, not just produce one

slides.title: Accept, reject, resample — the rejection-sampling trick
slides.body: The target model doesn't just check if the draft's top guess matches — it compares full probability distributions, token by token, using a rejection-sampling rule that keeps the final output mathematically identical to sampling from the target model alone.
bullets: Step 1: accept a draft token if the target model agrees it's plausible under its own distribution
Step 2: at the first disagreement, discard that draft token and resample it from a corrected distribution
Step 3: discard everything the draft proposed after that first rejection — it was conditioned on a token that never happened
This guarantees no quality loss: the math proves the output is drawn from the same distribution as standard decoding

slides.title: Worked example: 4 guesses, 2 survive
slides.body: Prompt: 'The capital of France is'. The draft model proposes 4 tokens ahead: ['Paris', ',', 'a', 'city']. The target model checks all 4 in one pass.
bullets: 'Paris' — target agrees, accepted
',' — target agrees, accepted
'a' — target disagrees (it preferred 'known'), so this token is rejected and resampled as 'known'
'city' — discarded, since it was generated assuming 'a' was correct
Net result: 3 verified tokens ('Paris', ',', 'known') produced from one target-model pass, instead of 3 separate passes

slides.title: Where the speedup comes from — and where it doesn't
slides.body: The win scales with how often the draft model guesses right, and it only applies when the GPU has spare compute capacity to begin with.

rows: GPU compute utilization at batch size 1
Predictable text — code, boilerplate, common phrases
Novel, creative, or high-entropy text — low acceptance rate

slides.title: When NOT to reach for speculative decoding
slides.body: It's not a free lunch — the benefit depends heavily on the serving setting and the draft model's quality.
bullets: At large batch sizes, the GPU is already compute-bound, so there's little idle capacity left to absorb verification — the speedup shrinks or disappears
A poorly matched draft model (different vocabulary, very different style) gets rejected constantly, wasting the extra compute spent drafting
Running a second model means extra GPU memory and engineering complexity — not worth it for throughput-oriented batch jobs
Highly creative or unpredictable generation (brainstorming, poetry) has lower acceptance rates than code or structured text

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Speculative decoding trades idle GPU compute for fewer sequential passes through the big model
A small draft model proposes tokens; the target model verifies them in parallel via rejection sampling
It's provably lossless — output quality matches plain decoding exactly
Biggest wins: low-batch, latency-sensitive serving on predictable text like code
Smallest wins: large-batch throughput serving, or creative/high-entropy generation

questions.prompt: What guarantees that speculative decoding doesn't degrade output quality compared to plain decoding?
options: The draft model is fine-tuned to match the target exactly
A rejection-sampling rule that makes the final token distribution identical to sampling from the target model alone
Outputs are checked by a human reviewer before being accepted
The target model only runs once per sentence instead of per token
questions.explanation: The accept/reject/resample procedure is a rejection-sampling scheme specifically designed so the resulting output distribution is mathematically identical to standard autoregressive decoding from the target model — it's a speed trick, not an approximation.

questions.prompt: In which serving scenario does speculative decoding help the LEAST?
options: Single-user chat with a predictable, code-heavy prompt
Low-latency assistants generating boilerplate text
Large-batch throughput serving where the GPU is already compute-bound
A draft model that closely matches the target model's style
questions.explanation: Speculative decoding works by using spare GPU compute capacity (normally idle during memory-bound, low-batch decoding) to verify multiple tokens at once. At large batch sizes, that compute headroom is already used up, so there's little left to absorb the extra verification work.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, the draft model proposed ['Paris', ',', 'a', 'city'] and the target model rejected 'a'. What happens to 'city'?
options: It's kept, since only 'a' was rejected
It's discarded, because it was generated assuming the rejected token 'a' was correct
It's resampled independently of 'a'
It's appended after the resampled replacement for 'a'
questions.explanation: Once a draft token is rejected, every token the draft model proposed after it is thrown away too — they were all generated conditioned on a token that turned out not to match the target model's distribution, so they're no longer valid continuations.

posts.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5 Outscores Opus on Agentic Coding

posts.summary: Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Sept 28, 2026) is positioned as the fast, cheap sibling of Opus 5.5 — but it actually beats Opus on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and nearly matches it on real-world knowledge work, all at unchanged per-token pricing. bullets: Sonnet 5.5 beats Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and nearly ties it on GDPval-AA Elo (1844 vs 1846)

posts.title: Nine Loops Deep: Claude Beats a Physics Record
posts.subtitle: A blog dare, a $100 Python script, and a scattering-amplitude calculation that went one loop past the 2023 record.
posts.summary: Physicist Matt von Hippel publicly dared AI labs to push a frontier scattering-amplitude calculation past its known limit on an academic budget. Anthropic researchers had Claude run for days inside Claude Science, reaching nine loops in planar N=4 super Yang-Mills theory — one loop past the 2023 record — for about $100-2,000, independently validated by the physicist who built the original method.

slides.title: A Blog Dare Became a Physics Record
slides.body: On August 7, 2026, physicist Matt von Hippel publicly challenged AI companies to solve a frontier scattering-amplitude problem using only the compute an academic could plausibly access.
bullets: The dare: push N=4 super Yang-Mills to nine loops, or N=8 supergravity to seven — either would beat the current record
Anthropic physicists Liam Fitzpatrick and Siddharth Mishra-Sharma took it on, running Claude inside Claude Science

slides.title: Why 'One More Loop' Is So Hard
slides.body: Scattering amplitudes predict how particles interact and get checked against experiments like the LHC. 'Loops' measure the complexity of the interaction being modeled — and the math explodes with every one.
bullets: Most real-world amplitudes have only been computed to 2 loops, a few to 3
The most precise physics prediction ever made (the electron's magnetic moment) used 5 loops
Lance Dixon's team set the prior record — 8 loops — in 2023, using a 'form factor' and 'antipodal duality' technique (arXiv:2308.08199)
Nine loops of the six-particle (hexagon) amplitude had never been computed by anyone before this

slides.title: What Claude Actually Did
slides.body: The researchers didn't hand Claude a new algorithm. They gave it the target, told it to keep working with periodic check-ins, and let it try both known approaches from scratch.
bullets: Claude (described as 'Fable 5.1') ran inside Claude Science, told to work autonomously and report back every 4-6 hours
It attempted the problem two ways: Dixon's original bootstrap method, and the newer indirect form-factor approach
It wrote all the calculation code itself, in Python with SymPy, from scratch
The bootstrap run cost roughly $100 — equivalent to about 96 CPUs running for a week; either full approach would cost an end user $1,000-$2,000

slides.title: 2023 Record vs. 2026 Result vs. a Concurrent Rival

rows: Bootstrap, written from scratch in Python/SymPy
Song He's group, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Reached within days of Claude's result

slides.title: Validated by the Person Who Invented the Method
slides.body: Anthropic didn't just publish Claude's number — they sent it to the one person best positioned to catch an error.
bullets: Fitzpatrick and Mishra-Sharma contacted von Hippel in late August to report progress
Lance Dixon — who built the bootstrap recipe decades of work rests on — checked the result and confirmed it on September 1, 2026
Dixon's addendum: Claude used his group's own 2019 and 2023 methods and presented the answer in the same format his team would have used
The full nine-loop result was published openly (smsharma.io/cosmic-nine-loops/) alongside the September 25 writeup

slides.title: What This Isn't
slides.body: Both von Hippel and Dixon were careful to draw a line between 'executed a known recipe faster' and 'discovered new physics.'
bullets: Von Hippel: Claude used known methods with more raw compute than anyone had thrown at the problem, plus possibly cleaner code — not a new insight
He explicitly calls it reliable and autonomous, but 'not super-intelligently' achieved
Dixon: the real milestone will be when a model proposes a genuinely new physical principle, not just a bigger, faster version of an existing one
Unclear how far the result generalizes to other amplitude problems — this is one theory (a 'toy model'), not a real-world prediction yet

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: A frontier physics calculation that used to need a specialist team's sustained effort got done for roughly the price of a dinner for two
Independent expert validation (Dixon) and a concurrent rival result (Song He's group) both corroborate the number — this isn't a one-source claim
The achievement is compute and engineering taste applied to a known recipe, not new scientific discovery — von Hippel suggests there may be more of this 'low-hanging fruit' than experts assumed
Expect more 'AI reproduces a hard-but-known result cheaply' stories before 'AI discovers a new principle' stories

posts.title: Claude Speeds Up 30 Biology Models by 4x
posts.subtitle: Custom FlashPairformer kernels let Claude fold a 70,000-token ribosome on one GPU node and design binders for $150 instead of $10,000.
posts.summary: Anthropic had Claude optimize more than 30 open-source biomolecular modeling tools over about four weeks, writing custom GPU kernels (FlashPairformer) that cut triangle-attention and triangle-multiplication costs by roughly 2-3x and enabled folding systems over 10,000 tokens on a single GPU node. A de novo protein-binder design run matched an earlier campaign's results using about 1% of the GPU hours.

slides.title: Claude Optimizes 30 Open-Source Biology Models
slides.body: Anthropic had Claude spend roughly four weeks optimizing structure-prediction, protein-design, protein-language, and genomics models — supervised by two staff with biology experience but no prior kernel-engineering background.
bullets: Published Sep 17, 2026 by Anthropic's Science team
Code open-sourced at github.com/anthropics/uplifting-biomolecular-modeling

slides.title: Triangle Attention Is a Cubic Bottleneck
slides.body: Protein structure-prediction models spend most of their compute and memory on 'triangle attention' and 'triangle multiplication' — operations that scale cubically with system size.
bullets: Doubling the size of a molecular system costs roughly 8x more time and memory under cubic scaling
Optimizing these kernels has traditionally taken experienced engineers weeks per model
Large systems like molecular machines often needed multiple GPU nodes just to run at all

slides.title: FlashPairformer: Kernels Claude Wrote From Scratch
slides.body: Claude built a set of custom kernels for triangle attention and multiplication, plus general optimizations, and applied them across the model suite in under four weeks.
bullets: Average ~4x speedup with minimal precision loss; close to 2x (1.6x in one benchmark) with bit-identical outputs
Techniques used: custom CUDA-style kernels, caching redundant recomputed work, collapsing dead branches into constant outputs
Applied across 30+ models spanning structure prediction, protein design, protein language modeling, and genomics

slides.title: Folding a Ribosome on One GPU Node
slides.body: The optimizations unlocked a 'big, low-memory' mode that pushes past what was previously practical on a single node.
bullets: Accurately folded systems over 10,000 tokens on one NVIDIA GPU node, with successful inference past 70,000 tokens
Examples folded: human mitochondrial complex I, the TRiC chaperone, a proteasome, and a bacterial ribosome
For scale: AlphaFold3 accurately predicted a 40S ribosome at 7,663 tokens — these systems go well beyond that

slides.title: Where It Still Falls Short
slides.body: The post is explicit about the limits, not just the wins.
bullets: On an 8-GPU B300 node, attempts at very large assemblies (31,000-70,000+ tokens, like viral capsids) were NOT predicted correctly — attributed to poor generalization beyond training context, not a kernel-speed problem
Fast modes were only verified 'statistically indistinguishable' from defaults on a pooled benchmark set (DockQ > 0.23 threshold) — not guaranteed for every possible input
Two experienced human supervisors were still required throughout; this isn't a fully autonomous, unsupervised pipeline

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: A general-purpose model, not a specialized compiler, closed most of the gap to hand-tuned GPU kernels across 30+ scientific models in under a month
The 'big, low-memory' mode turns some multi-node jobs into single-node jobs — a real accessibility shift for smaller academic labs
Protein-binder design costs dropped roughly 60-70x for comparable results, though very large assemblies still fail — the gains aren't uniform across problem sizes
